speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is the Prime Minister going to make a statement?

I have a statement to make but it seemed to me that it might be more convenient it I made it when the house was in committee because then questions could be asked and answered to elucidate the statement and to give such further information as I might have available. There is another reason for my preference to do it that way. This is a motion under standing order 60 and that standing order provides:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
The motion being moved at this time is merely a motion that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair so that the standing order can be complied with. There cannot at this stage or until the committee has considered the resolution be any vote of the house upon its substance. So that it would not seem to be in accord with the standing order to discuss at this time the merits or demerits of the resolution. That has to be considered first of all in committee before there can be any expression of opinion by the house upon its merits or demerits.
I do not want to start a long discussion about procedure at this time, but I think it is a matter worthy of consideration. There is the practical advantage that if I make my statement when the house is in committee hon. members will have the opportunity of asking me for further information about any points I may be suggesting in support of the resolution.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that this is a most important subject and it is desirable to proceed upon the basis of a statement from the government as to its general intention. I am certainly of the impression that when we have had similar motions before us in regard to other matters statements have been made and that it has been customary for other members to express their opinions in regard to the matter under consideration.
I would point out that if a statement is made now by the Prime Minister (Mr. St.
tMr. St. Laurent.]
Laurent) as to the general intention of the government in connection with this important matter it will then be possible for hon. members to ask questions when we have gone into committee. I think what should be borne in mind in connection with this is that the subject matter is something about which I am sure there is no dispute. I feel sure that all hon. members welcome the decision to proceed with something which has been requested for a great many years.
I think it would be helpful if hon. members had a statement from the government as to the way in which they propose to proceed with this matter. Doubtless other hon. members besides myself will wish to say something in the light of what the Prime Minister would say. Then, if the motion is adopted, as I trust it will be unanimously, it will be possible to ask any question that may suggest itself when we have proceeded into committee. I respectfully ask the Prime Minister to follow that course.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that it would take some time perhaps to reach a definite decision as to what standing order 60 really means because of the practice which has grown up in the past I have no objection to making my statement now. But I make it under reserve of my request to His Honour the Speaker to consider standing order 60 and at some future time give us the benefit of his opinion as to its proper construction.
As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has said, I am sure that there will be no one in this house who will not consider that this matter is of sufficient importance to warrant taking up the time of the committee of the whole to consider whether a bill should be introduced. I think it is safe to assume that all members of the house will be glad to see some step made toward the realization of a national library for the Canadian nation. I think it is also safe to say that there was nothing included in the speech by which His Excellency opened this parliament which was more decidedly commended than- the announcement that there would be introduced at this time legislation preliminary to the establishment of a national library.
The leader of the opposition is right in saying that for some time past a number of requests have been made that steps be taken toward establishing this kind of public service for the Canadian people. Late in 1946 a brief was presented to the government by a group of societies, including the Canadian Library Asssociation, the Royal Society of Canada and others, asking that the first

preliminary steps toward the organization of a national library in Canada should be taken at the earliest moment.
In September, 1948, the newly appointed dominion archivist was given the special assignment of preparing the way for the establishment of a national library, and a national library advisory committee was appointed under his chairmanship. On the advice of this committee the government approved the establishment in 1950 of the bibliographic centre which was intended to be the first unit of the national library. This centre is temporarily located in the public archives building.
Then in 1949 the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences was appointed and asked to consider the national library question. The purpose of the bill to follow this resolution is to carry into effect the recommendation of the royal commission that a national library be established without delay.
Just a word about the present plan. The bill to be introduced if the committee approves the resolution will give ample authority for the organization of a full-fledged national library. Of course this is not something that is going to be realized overnight. It may be that under existing conditions some time must necessarily pass before the project is well advanced in implementation. In the first place, defence requirements make the immediate construction of a new building impracticable for the time being and a national library cannot function with maximum benefit to the community without suitable quarters.
In the second place a great amount of cataloguing of books and other preliminary work must be done before the national library itself can begin to lend books, to give an adequate reference service to inquirers and perform other functions of a public library. It is this essential preliminary work which the government is proposing should be pushed forward immediately, in the hope that the day when a suitable building can be erected will not be too far distant.
I should like now to say a word as to the character of the library. Hon. members who have read the recommendations of the advisory committee which was tabled on March 3 last, and which the government has accepted in principle, will know that the proposed national library promises to be somewhat different in character from the national libraries in many other countries.
It is axiomatic that no modern government can function without books, and the government of Canada is no exception. Since no national library has been in existence, essential book needs have had to be met from other
National Library
sources. The library of parliament has done its best to fill partially that gap, and the public archives have for many years been performing services normally associated with a national library rather than with archives. Many of the department libraries came into existence originally because there was no national library to furnish the services that were necessary. It is not proposed that the new national library should absorb all these collections, but that it should complement them where needed, and by pooling their catalogues should make them into a more closely knit library system so that what is already in existence elsewhere will become available to those who might require the information from those books through the national library.
In making its plans for the national library the government has assumed that there will be the closest possible co-operation between the new library, the library of parliament, the libraries of government departments and agencies, and also between the national library and many of the public libraries throughout the country. We want to reduce to a minimum unnecessary duplication. For example, there is no thought of building up new scientific collections that would rival or duplicate those already in the library of the national research council. Those books will be included, however, in the general catalogue, and on proper occasions they will be made available through the services of the national library to students who may require to consult them.
One basic objective of any national library, I think, is to become the most comprehensive library in the world on its own country. It is proposed that Canada's national library should try to reach that objective, but that in working towards that end it should co-operate with other government libraries, and with a large number of other institutions throughout Canada. The bill to be introduced, if and when the resolution is adopted, will contain a deposit law. The Massey report recommends that the national library should secure as complete a collection as possible of books published in Canada, books published by Canadians and of books on Canadian themes, all to the end that it might be the most comprehensive collection of books in the world relating to Canada.
In other countries corresponding publications are secured mostly under the provisions of their respective copyright or deposit laws which require the publishers to send copies of new books, pamphlets or maps and so forth to the national library. The proposed bill would establish a deposit system in

National Library
Canada, but perhaps not as stringent and rigorous as the systems that exist elsewhere, at least not initially.
This deposit requirement is not entirely new. There is already a partial requirement for deposit under section 11 of the Copyright Act amendment of 1931, which directs that two copies of every work copyrighted in Canada should be sent to the library of parliament. In drafting this bill, care has been taken to avoid any clash between the copyright provision and the intended provision with respect to deposit under the new act. A deposit law supplementary to the copyright law is, I think, very desirable, because a considerable number of publications which the national library will wish to secure and preserve are not formally protected under the copyright act. Some of them could not be copyrighted as they consist mainly of material already in the public domain.
With respect to imported books, the government is well aware of the large proportion of books, listed on the catalogues of Canadian publishing firms, which are printed in other countries and imported into Canada. Most of these originate in Great Britain, in France and in the United States. Those publications number many thousands each year, and although they are published in Canada, in the sense that they are released here for public distribution or sale, the firms handling them are actually acting more in the capacity of agents than publishers. It seems to me it would be unfair to claim two free copies of all these thousands of titles, and it is proposed that regulations will be made under the new legislation which will provide suitable exemptions and will, in fact, confine the deposit requirements to books wholly or partially produced in Canada, books published by Canadian authors and books the contents of which relate in some significant way to Canadian affairs.
To cite a theoretical example, a history of Canada published in Great Britain and imported through an agency in Canada for distribution and sale would have to be sent to the national library. A history of China, however, similarly published outside of Canada and of which some copies might be imported for distribution, would not be required to be deposited in the national library.
It may be well to point out at once that the deposit provision in the proposed bill is much less onerous than similar provisions existing in many other countries. In France, where the law of deposit has been in effect for more than four hundred years, both the printer and the publisher must deposit copies

and an additional copy must be sent in every time the book is reprinted, even though the reprint may not contain any new material. In Great Britain, where deposit is made under a copyright law, as many as six copies may be requested. The Oxford university library, the Cambridge university library, the national library of Scotland and other institutions have, by law, the right to claim copies under the British Copyright Act.
By contrast, the bill we propose to introduce would require a maximum of two copies, and if the work exceeds a certain retail value this requirement is reduced to one copy. The retail value suggested is $25. If the retail value of a book is more than $25, the requirement provided by the bill would be that the deposit of one copy would be sufficient.
I should like to say a word about the union catalogue. I believe that one of the most important duties of the proposed national library will be the preparation of a union catalogue. As this name implies, it is a catalogue in which the individual catalogues of many libraries will be combined in a single alphabetical system. Work on such a program has been in progress in Ottawa for the last two years.
The catalogues of most of the libraries ini Ottawa are now included and those of half a dozen important collections elsewhere have been either completely secured or partially secured. The ultimate aim is to build up a -complete key to the contents of every important collection- of books in Canada, With such a catalogue -in its possession the national library will be able to -tell anyone in the matter -of a few minutes whether a copy of any particular book is to be found in -Canada, and if one exists, the name of the library in which it is located. It is hoped that there will be organized a service whereby the national library will be able to have that book sent here so that it may be available -to the inquirer.
The national library would have the task of preparing and maintaining a national bibliography. By that, -as hon. members know, is meant a complete and systematic listing of all new publications issued in Canada, written by Canadians or relating in any important way to this country. Work on -this project has been in progress since the beginning of 1951, and the bibliography is already being published monthly under the title of Canadiana. I should like to table a complete set of the monthly -bulletins that have been issued so that hon. members may see that already a great deal of valuable work of lasting benefit to the Canadian public has been accomplished by this germ

of our national library, with the modest funds that have so far been voted by parliament to that end.
The bill proposes to continue in a formal way the somewhat informal national library advisory committee which has been in existence since 1948-49. This committee has over the last three or four years been meeting twice a year, and it is not anticipated that the new advisory council would need to meet more frequently than a couple of times a year. It is proposed that it be made up of twelve members, that there be at least one member for each of the ten Canadian provinces, and two others selected at large.
As to the operating policy, it may be well to note that ultimately the new national library is intended to serve both the government and the public. The value to the government is obvious enough. But the library is also planned to serve any citizen of Canada who has need of the information available in the national library itself, or in one of the libraries throughout Canada represented in the union catalogue.
Service to the public will normally be given through another library. If, for example, a person residing in Vancouver has need for certain books that are in the library in Ottawa, he will apply to the Vancouver public library or to the library of the university of British Columbia, and the librarian there would borrow the books from the national library here, instead of the national library here sending them direct to the inquirer. By arranging the loan in this way, the responsibility for borrowing the material will be taken by an institution which knows the person concerned and which will be in a position to supervise his use of the book and to make reasonably sure that no abuses will be committed in that way. I think there is already a mutual arrangement between the university of British Columbia and two or three United States universities whereby their joint library treasures are available to the public of the various communities they serve, and that it is done in that way.
The Canadian Library Association has emphasized many times the importance of having adequate photo-duplicating equipment available in a national library. The reason they give is that many requests will be received for rare or valuable books, or for material which it would not be prudent to allow out of the premises. Photographic copies of these, which can- be made very cheaply, would be furnished instead of the books themselves. Such a procedure would safeguard our rare books and yet make their contents available to those who have a real interest in securing such information. I understand that that is also something which 55704-150
National Library
has had the benefit of practical experience in other institutions where union catalogues are used.
With respect to a building, the proposed legislation has been modelled in large part on the legislation respecting the national gallery which was enacted at the last session of parliament. The gallery, of course, is a corporation having its own board of trustees whilst, under the proposal to be submitted following the adoption of this resolution, the library will be under the direct responsibility of a minister of the crown, the national librarian and the assistant national librarian, but its operations will be largely parallel to those of the national gallery. This will also probably be true in the case of building policy.
The government last year authorized the board of trustees of the national gallery to take appropriate steps looking to the erection of an appropriate building to house the national gallery. Hon. members know that a competition for the selection of an architect has been established by the board of governors of the national gallery. The site for the national gallery has been selected. The site that has been selected is Cartier square where are to be found the temporary buildings now housing much of the Department of National Defence. This competition gives every promise of having excited the interest of the best architectural talent in Canada. The competition is to run until the autumn. It is a competition not necessarily to select the plans for the gallery but to select the architect who will draw the plans; and it is expected that the sketches that will be submitted in this preliminary competition will reveal to the board examining the sketches the qualities of the architect who will prepare them, and his competence or otherwise to carry out the undertaking of providing a suitable national gallery.
There has been no definite selection of a site for the library, but the report suggests that an appropriate site might be on the banks of the Ottawa river at the end of Bank street where a building could be erected with several storeys below the street level, which building would provide valuable and reasonably safe stack space and would be connected with the library of parliament by an underground passage that would provide a physical connection between the two places where the books were being kept. That question has not yet been definitely decided, but it is hoped that it will be possible at an early date to select at least tentatively an appropriate site for a building.
The present thought is that it would be desirable to have a competition open to all

National Library
Canadian architects to submit sketches from which selection of an architect to prepare the plans could be made, and that the plans could be got ready, so that, as soon as circumstances warranted the expenditure and the use of the manpower and material for the erection of the appropriate building, it could be proceeded with and the hazards to which this valuable collection housed in the parliamentary library are subject could be substantially diminished. There is great congestion in the parliamentary library. It contains many many books that could not be replaced at any cost, and I think it is desirable to look upon the provision of proper safekeeping for these treasures as a matter worthy of pretty high priority.
With respect to administration, the bibliographic centre and such national library activities as are being carried on at the present time are conducted under the direction of the dominion archivist. If this proposal meets with the approval of parliament, it is the intention to make the dominion archivist the national librarian, and to continue the policy of developing the national library under his supervision.
The Massey commission expressed the opinion that ultimately the national library and the public archives should develop separately under independent heads. That may be desirable, but the commission went on to say, however, that it felt "it would be unsuitable at this time to break the personal union between the (bibliographic) centre and the archives." And I think some practical experience of joint administration of these two services would appear to be desirable before there is any policy determined with finality with respect to separating them.
There are a good many points in favour of the closest possible relationship between the national library and the public archives, perhaps particularly in view of the special conditions under which we find ourselves here in Canada, and of the fact that public archives are the material upon which many of the books that will come in future into the national library will be based.
In order that the national library may adequately serve the needs of those who habitually work in both official languages, it is proposed to make the first assistant national librarian at this time French-speaking because the librarian will be English-speaking. It is hoped that that kind of precedent would be considered seriously with respect to future appointments. I think it might very well be, as provided in 'the rules of this house, that the principal assistant to the librarian be
IMr. St. Laurent.]
perfectly familiar with the tongue which is not the mother tongue of the librarian.
There is also a provision in the estimates for a small amount for continuing this bibliographic centre's work. It is probable that if the house looks favourably upon this proposal there will have to be another modest provision made in the supplementary estimates. It would be a provision that would be substantially below $100,000 this year; but the amount that is already provided in the estimates would not appear to be sufficient to do what the dominion archivist feels could be accomplished to good purposes at the present time.
I hope that the reaction of all hon. members to this proposal will be much like the reaction of the press since the introduction of the resolution has been announced in the press, and that everyone would feel that this is a matter of national consequence that should be proceeded with with reasonable dispatch and should have among the civilian activities of the Canadian people a high priority.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated
earlier, I am sure that all hon. members will welcome the first step in what would appear to be the fulfilment of a dream that has engaged the imagination and the hopes of Canadians for a very long time.
Ever since this country became one nation at confederation there have been repeated suggestions that a national library would be in keeping with the status and dignity of the nation which had been brought together in that way. One of the things which undoubtedly present a special problem is that the very size of the country itself makes it difficult to determine exactly how far a national library will go in providing books which will be available for all Canadians in every part of Canada.
It is inevitable that a very large proportion of the people of Canada will not find it possible to avail themselves of whatever facilities are provided in the city of Ottawa. For that reason it would seem of very great importance that from the very beginning the thought should always be in the minds of those who are planning the procedure and acquiring the books that whatever is done should be done in a way that will, on the one hand, establish a library truly national in its structure and in the contents of that library itself, and at the same time make it something that as far as possible is available to all Canadians who seek the opportunity to gain knowledge from the books that are stored here and made available under some procedure such as that outlined by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent).

If anyone examines the things that have been said about libraries he will find that there are two very widely separated points of view. To the cynic, a library is merely a cemetery of books. To the person who wishes to dominate the minds of the people, a library is a danger. We have seen in recent years that those who sought to set up dictatorships in different countries in Europe and elsewhere burned some of the great library collections so that those thoughts which might in themselves give heart and vigour to the people who loved freedom would disappear from the country. That has gone on for many centuries, and we read of the similar destruction of libraries even as long as 2,000 years ago. It does seem, therefore, that what is essential in planning this library is that at the outset there be a very clear understanding of the real function of this library in the national life of Canada, and the manner in which it will be made available to the people generally.
A library can either be a mere cemetery of books or it can be a repository of the living thought of the ages depending upon the procedure that is followed in establishing a direct contact between that library and the people themselves. The great task of the highly skilled librarian is to develop an interest in the books of the library, to keep before the people the availability of those books and to encourage their use for whatever purposes they may be sought.
The Prime Minister has spoken of the cataloguing of the books and the setting up of appropriate plans which will lay the foundation for the future acquisition of books throughout the years ahead, A clear determination now of what is to be placed in the national library, and what is to be acquired for that library, as distinguished from the many great public libraries across the country is essential at this time.
I was very interested in the Prime Minister's statement that, following the recommendations of the advisory committee, it was hoped that a site such as that which could be found at the end of Bank street, on the banks of the Ottawa river, might be chosen; because it would then be possible to connect that library by a passage to the library of parliament. In those words the Prime Minister answered a question I had in my own mind. I was interested to know what the future of the library of parliament was to be, and I take the statement he has made as an indication that the library of parliament is to be continued, and that its work will be closely associated with that of the national library. I believe members of parliament will welcome that information, because 55704-1504
National Library
it would be a great inconvenience to them if those books which are normally required by members were not readily available in this building.
On the other hand I am sure there are in the parliamentary library at this time precious volumes it would be wise to move to the new national library building, for purpose of safekeeping. One of the points raised in the report of the Massey commission is that there are in the parliamentary -library extremely valuable volumes which are not adequately protected against the danger of fire.
Also at this time I should like to pay my own tribute, one in which I feel sure every member of parliament will join, to the librarians and the staff of the parliamentary library. I feel sure that every member of the House of Commons has shared my experience in this respect. It would be impossible anywhere to find greater courtesy, greater industry and a greater desire to be of service to the members when they seek information which can be obtained in that library. I have had some experience with libraries in different places, and I must say that I have been deeply impressed with the way in which the librarians, and those associated with them here, are able to find quotations and references in a very short space of time, when requisitions are made to them with a sufficient indication of what is really sought to make it possible for them to use their excellent indexing system. I mention this not only to pay a well-deserved- tribute to these splendid public servants, but also simply to emphasize the fact that in building up a national library here we have the advantage of long years of experience and a skilled staff close at hand who can be of immense help in considering the plans that should be made in connection with the early purchases for the new library, and the plans for acquisitions to be made in future years.
I was happy to hear what the Prime Minister said with regard- to the preparation of a union catalogue. In this vast country-and sometimes I think we are inclined to forget how vast it is-there is great difficulty in integrating activities of a similar nature. Nevertheless it is doubtful if anything could be more helpful to Canadian students of all ages than a union catalogue which will make it possible for them, to learn where they can obtain information on any subject in which they m-ay be interested.
The Prime Minister touched upon an important point when he referred to the close association of the archives with a national

National Library
library. The archives will provide a considerable amount of material which can be used by those Canadians who will write our own history and those works of fiction which, in themselves, in due course become a part of our history.
There are many exciting examples of what our archives have already meant to us. For that reason I should like to recall what seems to me to be one of the most romantic examples of the value of public archives well indexed under various subheadings, so that people may know where to seek certain information. I mention this only in the hope that this particular part of our recent history in Canada may stand as a challenge to the imagination of Canadian youth, when they are told that they will have available to them not only the archives but a national library of this kind.
Our thoughts have been directed in recent years, and in most dramatic circumstances, to the importance of uranium and the various products of pitchblende. For that reason it is of more than passing interest to Canadians to recall how the great radium mine on Great Bear lake came to be discovered. Only a few days ago in the house, in an entirely different type of discussion, reference was made to the fact that the Eldorado mine was discovered by those who had been associated with a gold mine that had ceased to operate profitably, with the result that they had begun to seek a new mining property. It is not very often that a mining company finding itself near the end of its resources in one area goes out and succeeds in finding another mine. These men were looking for another gold mine. They found something that turned out to be infinitely more important, but the way in which they came to find it has a direct bearing on the importance of archives and the indexing not only of the contents of the archives but of the national library which is to be associated with it.
When Gilbert La Bine decided to seek a new mine he recalled having heard something about the discoveries of Samuel Hearne in the Arctic when he was travelling through that region in the 1760's. Hie recalled some reference to mineral deposits in that northern region. He came here and in the archives at Ottawa he found a reference to evidence of a shining metal that Hearne had seen on a promontory which might well be on the shores of Great Bear lake. It was for that reason that he engaged the services of one of the great pioneer bush pilots to fly him to the shores of Great Bear lake. There he sought the mineral deposits of which Hearne had written so many years before.
IMr. Drew.]
Of course there was no map at the time Hearne was there which even gave an indication of that enormous lake in the distant northland which is larger than lake Ontario or lake Erie. They were leaving the area in which they had sought to find a mine and were flying south at a time when the sun was fairly low. They saw the gossan which indicated mineral deposits. It was approaching the time of the freeze-up. They flew farther south and then arranged for dog teams. They went back, and to make an exciting story of Canadian adventure short they found what would appear to be the very mineral outcroppings that Hearne had seen so long ago. That discovery became one of the vital factors in Canada's important part in the recent struggle for freedom.
I mention that incident because it is quite possible that hidden in the archives at this very time there may be other equally interesting references from the past which may well be the guiding star for some Canadian of imagination and enterprise at some time in the future. But whether it be in the field of material achievement as in the case of the discovery of the Eldorado mine or whether it be in the achievements of the mind which in the years ahead will be still more important, the archives and the library will lay the foundation for Canadian development and for the improvement of the life of the country in its most important aspects.
The Prime Minister has spoken of the possibility of employing photography to make copies of important documents. I would hope that those documents which are distinctly a part of the early history of Canada would be photographed and made available in all the main libraries throughout Canada. It can be done at moderate expense and in a way that will make all the information available while [DOT]leaving the original documents safely in Ottawa under the type of protection which should be afforded to the basic history of Canada.
In this respect may I recall that our history has been closely associated with the building up of collections of books. So far as I can ascertain, the first collection of books that might be regarded as a real library was to be found in the early settlement of Port Royal about 1606. It was a private collection which became a source of great satisfaction to the people of the community in those early days. I understand that the first lending library of which there is a record was one established in Quebec by the Jesuit fathers who created a library of some 2,000 volumes. The very existence of these libraries indicates the extent to which those who built the country paid

attention to the importance of books and literature in the building of the culture and fabric of the nation.
In more recent years what are described as free libraries have become commonplace throughout the whole of Canada. At this time there are nearly 700 public libraries throughout Canada circulating close to 25 million volumes of books a year without charge. These are circulated to approximately 1,200,000 registered borrowers. One of the things I should like to emphasize in this connection is how much we are all indebted to the unselfish service of librarians throughout Canada who too often have not received the remuneration that their great responsibilities really merit. I sometimes think that perhaps we have not emphasized sufficiently the great extent to which the librarians in each community are responsible for the quality of the reading of the people of the community. They are not only the individuals who hand out books that are requested but they are the individuals whose advice is sought respecting the type of books that should be read so far as particular subjects are concerned. Their advice is sought frequently in regard to the general type of reading that should be undertaken, and particularly in the case of our children we are greatly indebted to the unselfish service of these librarians across Canada who without very much regard to the amount of money they receive have performed a great service in advancing the culture of this country.
Mr. Speaker, up to this time Canada has been one of the few countries of our stature, wealth and general development which have not been able to claim a national library. Perhaps in times gone by it was thought that there were other things that called for more immediate attention, but after all a library does provide the bread and butter for the mind. In the long history of human conflict the inspired thoughts to be found in the books which record the history of nations have provided the inspiration for the preservation of the things that we thought were worth while. Without in any way seeking to place more importance on one man than upon any other, I should like before closing my remarks to suggest that perhaps there is no case on record where a nation owed so much to libraries as did Great Britain in the days of the war just past.
In this respect 1 apply my remarks particularly to one man. Perhaps it may be some encouragement to many students today, particularly students who at this time are looking forward to impending examinations without too much confidence, to learn that the greatest writer of this day in the
National Library
English tongue, perhaps the greatest writer of English apart from Shakespeare, was a most uncertain and unsatisfactory student at school. It is a matter of record that Winston Churchill developed his facility in English and his capacity for writing from a collection of books which had been sent to him in India from a library at a time when he wanted to fill in the spare moments he had out there.
In his reading, we are told, particularly of history, he laid the foundation for a grasp of history that qualified him, not only as the greatest historian of our day but as a man whose every act has been inspired by the confidence that has come from the record of history throughout the years. I like to think that at the time when all the arithmetic of war made it clear that there was no reason for Great Britain to survive in the spring of 1940 it was knowledge gained from the pages of history, which was in Churchill's mind, that right has given might in the years that have passed, that gave him the fortitude and courage and spirit to give leadership to the whole free world in those desperate days.
The words that he spoke to the British people and to the people of the whole world over the radio at that time came from the pages of history. Even those classic words "blood, sweat and tears" came from an ancient volume which he had read long years before. The thoughts of those who built this nation are thoughts that should be carried into the mind of every Canadian. The high hopes, the great aspirations and the clear moral purpose that inspired our forefathers in the building of this country can best be passed on to the youth of Canada and to the coming generations by making available to them in this way the best that is past and the succeeding thoughts of the present.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all members of the house join in expressing appreciation of the moving of a resolution which foreshadows the establishment in Canada of a national library. I think it has long been a reflection on our national life that Canada was one of the few important nations in the world without a national library. The Massey report made a recommendation which is being carried out, at least in part, today. It was:
That a national library be established without delay; that a librarian be appointed as soon as may be expedient: that the national library advisory committee be reconstituted as a board of trustees of the national library with the librarian as chairman ex officio; that the librarian be charged with the direction of the bibliographic centre which shall be responsible through the librarian to the board of trustees.

National Library
That is substantially the intent of the resolution before the house. As hon. members know, I have long been interested in the establishment of a national library. Indeed during the war, when there was some discussion of a suitable war memorial for Canada, I suggested on more than one occasion that the time had arrived when we might establish as a memorial, not a pile of stone but something that might be regarded as a cultural centre for a national library, a national gallery and a national theatre.
If I had been asked at that time to suggest a suitable site for such a memorial I would have suggested a site in the neighbourhood of the present printing bureau, after that bureau had been removed, and close to the archives. However, this afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) suggested another site near the supreme court building. I believe that suggestion is a particularly good one. As the Prime Minister pointed out, there are physical features to that site which would make it possible to house, to care for and to protect valuable books. It would also be in close proximity to the parliamentary library. I understand that in connection with the heating system there is a partly completed tunnel which would provide quick means of transporting books between the national library and the parliamentary library as such books were required.
I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and the Prime Minister that there should be no thought of displacing the parliamentary library as the library of parliament. I join with other members of the house in expressing personal appreciation to the librarian and the staff of the present parliamentary library. I wonder how they can carry on with the very inadequate facilities that exist. A short time ago I read that when the library was built it was built to accommodate some 60,000 volumes. I am told that today nearly three-quarters of a million volumes are housed somehow in and under the parliamentary library. Anyone who has gone into the basement or the vaults, as they are called, under the present library, with its wooden shelves and structural inadequacies, must be impressed with the danger to the very valuable volumes that are housed beneath the floor of the present library of parliament, and indeed which occupy the shelves of the library itself. Consequently, in the interest of the preservation of the valuable volumes for future generations, it is well I believe that we are taking this initial step to establish a modern fireproof library in Canada.
I hope that, while this establishes a national library, thought is being given to the building of a national gallery more suitable than the

rather dismal and dark halls in which the very valuable pictures owned by Canada are housed today, and that we may be able to round that off in the not too distant future with a national theatre where drama, opera, symphony and cultural activities of that description may be available to the Canadian people, and perhaps through the magic of television carried from that central theatre to even the remote parts of this country. A library, then, is something that the nation requires, and I am sure it will receive public support. I believe it was significant that when the Massey commission on arts, letters and sciences was hearing representations some 90 or 100 briefs were submitted by organizations pointing out the desirability of founding a national library for Canada. In that library could be gathered together the important books of the nation.
I understand that today many of the important volumes are scattered in various departments. I am told that there are something like 200,000 books and valuable pamphlets housed beneath the supreme court building. I am told that there are thousands of books scattered around the departments of government and with the national research council. Not all of those books need be included in a national library, but undoubtedly many of them are volumes that should find a suitable place in a library of this description. I hope that that library will contain all kinds of books. I am a bit alarmed when I hear about the censorship of books. I think a good case can be made out for preventing the circulation of salacious and pornographic literature, but when I look over the list of books I see, for example, books that may be instructive to us or contain warning of the dangers to our way of life which are banned from entry into Canada. If I may mention one without, I am sure, being misunderstood, there is the "Problems of Leninism", by Joseph Stalin.
Now, if we are going to fight Stalinism, if we are going to fight Leninism and communism, we have to know something about them. I am a bit leery of preventing the importation into this country of books which deny to us an understanding of the kind of thing that we may have to fight in Canada. I remember very well reading during my student days, and subsequently, Milton's great work pleading for freedom from censorship, called "Areopagitica"; that plea still lingers in my memory. I remember the remarks of Voltaire when he saw his books being burnt on the streets of Paris. He said, "They can burn my books but they cannot burn my ideas."

I say to the house that I hope in a national library there will be no limitation as to the kind of books that are included in that library, so that students may get a complete understanding of what we may have to cope with in the future and may not be blinded by some kind of censorship. If I may recount a personal experience, some few years ago-I have forgotten the year but about 1924 or 1925-I had a friend in the city of Regina who sent to a secondhand book dealer in Great Britain for a number of books. When these books arrived one was missing. Upon inquiry he was told that the book had been sent back to Ottawa to see if it was fit for importation into Canada. The book was entitled "Socialism, Critical and Constructive", by James Ramsay MacDonald, who had been a prime minister of the United Kingdom. Consequently, when we have any sort of censorship we should make sure that the matter is gone into very thoroughly and very carefully, and those who exercise the censorship should not be, for example, an overworked minister of the crown, as an answer to a question I placed on the order paper indicated yesterday, but persons who are both thoroughly competent and who can devote the necessary time to making an appraisal of the books that may be suggested for censorship.
As I said, the parliamentary library lacks a good many modern facilities today, facilities for students who want to use the library- yes, even for members of parliament. Sometimes members of parliament find it difficult when they go into the library to consult volumes to find a suitable place where they can be quiet and alone to conduct the research they desire to do. Ordinary comfort facilities for the staff are lacking in that library, and consequently we need something more modern. At the moment, we are getting copyright books in the library and that should give us a complete set of the volumes written and published in Canada for which copyright is taken. But as the Prime Minister said, there are written and published outside of Canada many books which deal with Canadian affairs. They should be assembled, cared for and catalogued.
I understand that the work of cataloguing the library has been going on for a couple of years, but it is still incomplete. Moreover, what we need is a catalogue not only of the books in our own national library and parliamentary library but a catalogue of the books scattered around the country in many other libraries. There are some wonderful volumes here and there across Canada. A year or two ago when I was in Fredericton the legislative librarian said she would like
National Library
to show me one of their great treasures. I was shown one of the few large authentic copies of the Doomsday book. That is a treasure for which the province of New Brunswick cares, but which would find a place in a catalogue of valuable volumes in Canada. I also saw one of the original copies of the Audubon series of books, illustrated.
I think it is regrettable that in so many of our provinces, in years gone by, we have not had a library or archives where the letters and books of some of the old-timers and settlers could have been assembled and kept for future generations.
In my own province of Saskatchewan I know that it has only been in the last few years that a competent archivist-and an exceedingly competent one, incidentally-has been appointed and when the records of that province which were lying scattered in the basement, subjected to destruction by mice, moths and other insects, have been properly assembled, sorted out and preserved for the benefit of future generations.
The archives and the library must work together. In this city I have spent days in the archives of Canada, although I have not been there lately. In it there are some wonderful volumes. We have there interesting letters, including correspondence of former prime ministers of Canada, some records of the early explorers and so on. I am happy indeed to hear the Prime Minister say that the present archivist is to be, at least temporarily, the chief librarian and that the two offices are to be combined in one exceedingly able and capable gentleman. I think that is an excellent idea.
I am also happy to support the Prime Minister in the suggestion that the assistant librarian should be one who speaks the language of the other great language group in Canada. As an English-speaking person myself, I realize that that is as it should be.
The leader of the opposition mentioned, as did the Prime Minister, the necessity of photographing documents. A great deal of microfilming has been done already in connection with the present library. With the modern microfilm and the modern process, it will not be necessary to pile up vast quantities of old newspapers. They can be microfilmed and still be available for generations yet to come.
I therefore think that this is a splendid project. I hope the government will be able to proceed with it as rapidly as possible. I hope that we may have a suitable building as soon as conditions permit. I also think that the idea of an advisory committee representative of all the provinces and the official language groups in our country is an excellent idea. I hope that that advisory committee

National Library
will be chosen by the government not because somebody would like to go on it from a certain city, perhaps a friend of the government in power-not necessarily this government, but succeeding governments-placed there as a sort of recognition of political support for a party in power. I would hope rather that persons will be chosen for that advisory committee because of their knowledge of and their interest in books and libraries. I think that is quite important.
Now I have said all that I wish to say, Mr. Speaker. I am speaking not only on my own behalf but on behalf of those associated with me when I say that we welcome this resolution and we hope that the idea will be brought to speedy fruition.
The leader of the opposition mentioned the great contribution that the Right Hon. Winston Churchill had made to the winning of the war because of his knowledge, and his gift in the use, of the English language. I do not think that fact can be overestimated. The more we can encourage our rising generation to understand their own language, be it French or be it English and to be able to speak their own language well, be it French or be it English, the better it will be. It would be better still, of course, for them to be able to speak both languages equally well, as does the Prime Minister, but they should be encouraged to understand at least their own mother tongue and to appreciate its beauties. French is a charming and beautiful language; English, too, is a stately and a beautiful language. Some of us look back over the years to our early training in the English tongue and realize how few were the books that we read. I often say that any gift I may possess I owe not only to my mother tongue but to my mother, at whose knee I learned the beauties of the English language through three simple books, namely the Bible, the Book of Common Prayer and the Pilgrim's Progress.

Mr. Speaker, this is one of those happy occasions on which all parties in the house find themselves in agreement. I am glad that in this particular instance it was on a resolution introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that we could find such happy agreement. We also welcome the resolution, containing as it does the program for the establishment in Canada of a national library.
We want to compliment the Prime Minister on the initial good progress that appears to have been made toward achieving the objective that is outlined in this resolution. From what he said this afternoon I think we can all feel quite happy about the progress that has been made.

At this moment, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up any great length of time because I am afraid that it would be merely repetition. I should like to leave the matter pretty much as it is, because the speeches that have been made this afternoon have been eloquent and have fairly well covered all phases of the problem that confronts us.
The suggestion that the site for the building be down at the end of Bank street is, I think, a happy one. It seems to me quite clear that the future of the parliamentary library has been assured. For the convenience of members of parliament I think it would be a good thing to have a connecting passage between the library of parliament and the new national library when it is completed. I therefore say that the suggestion that the site be at the end of Bank street down near the Ottawa river is a happy one. I have no better suggestion to offer. I can say that.
As to the advisory board which it is proposed to set up, I should like to make this suggestion. I think Alberta has a representative on the present board; but if my information is correct, that representative is not a well-known person interested in national libraries. Also, if I am correctly advised, that person has not attended the meetings of the board. I should like to see appointed from each province someone who has indicated in the past a real and sincere interest in the development of the national library and who will make it a point to attend meetings when they are called and to contribute, out of his experience, to the achievement of the fine objective that we have set before us.
In connection with the provision of a building, it must be remembered that we are a young country; and we do not want to repeat the experience that we have had with the parliamentary library. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has already pointed out, it was originally anticipated that the parliamentary library would perhaps accommodate 60,000 volumes. But today it is called upon to accommodate, to administer and to take care of something like 750,000 volumes. It seems quite clear that because we are a young country and have much time before us and great development ahead of us we ought to plan carefully so as to provide adequate space to take care of our needs for many many years to come.
I think that that is about the only suggestion I might make in connection with the provision of a building. I do feel, Mr. Speaker, *that there are many services which the *national library could extend to the people of Canada, and especially to the struggling community libraries all across this great country.

The idea of a union catalogue is a splendid one; in fact it is one which I am sure has within it a great many more good things and possibilities for our country that we now envision. I am very happy to learn that steps have already been taken to start the registration in such a union catalogue.
Let me just conclude by saying, Mr. Speaker, that we in this party feel that priority should be given to this great project, and that the work should go forward with that speed that is consistent with the importance of the project itself.

I cannot let this motion pass without saying a word or two on this subject, which is very dear to my heart. It is unusual to speak in an atmosphere of such accord, and I should simply like to endorse most, in fact I think nearly all, of the things which have been said by previous speakers. The only thing I might find fault with in what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said is that he said that existing conditions may cause some delay in the carrying out of the fulfilment of what has been up to the present a dream to many. I know it has been a dream of my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), ever since I have known him. As a matter of fact, before I was associated with him at all I heard him make a speech on this particular subject.
I was particularly interested in the Prime Minister's statement, and it is to that that I might address my remarks. The Prime Minister said there would be, he hoped, the closest co-operation of the new library with many of the public libraries throughout the country. That is perhaps one of the most important things that he said in his very pleasant announcement.
There has been a word or two of protest on the part of some of my correspondents as to the location of the national library. Their view was that perhaps Ottawa, with the national gallery and other cultural things, might be getting more than its share. I may say that my view does not coincide with that of those correspondents, because if we are to have a truly national library, then Ottawa is the place in which it will have to be built.
When I speak of the great assistance that a national library can be to outlying centres I would like to point out that most of our library facilities are in the city. That is no doubt natural but perhaps unfortunate. Libraries and books are to me, and I think to all of us, the greatest source of adult education. May I say, without any disparagement, that we are in need of adult education. It is true, as I said in another speech the other day, that 50 per cent of the people in Canada today have 55704-151
National Library
a grade VIII, that is a public school, education standard, or less. For a country with our potentialities, with our present wealth and potential resources, I do not think that is a good record. In these days one needs something better than a public school education, although many of the men who served this country best did not have anything more.
There is an unfortunate feeling around, and I think particularly among high school graduates, that those who attain the standing of a university entrance, or grade XII as it was called, have more or less completed their education. I think, sir, we should agree that they have only begun their education; that they have only become equipped with the tools through which they can gain an education for themselves which after all is the best way and the only way that one can gain it in any case.
I think reading is the greatest thing, the greatest asset, the greatest instrument of that education. We have not been noted as a nation of readers. I was looking through an interesting lot of statistics, a survey of libraries, issued by the government of Canada for
1948-50, and I was startled by some of the figures that I found there. I was looking at the summarized expenditures on public libraries for 1949. On page 9 I find for example- and I do not want to enter into any particular disparagement of any particular province; I can only give the figures as they come-that on books and periodicals the expenditure in the different provinces in the year 1949 was as follows. I will give merely the round figures. In Prince Edward Island, $6,000; Nova Scotia, $5,000; New Brunswick, $6,000; I shall now give some of the higher ones: Ontario, $582,711; Manitoba, $39,000; Saskatchewan, $36,000; Alberta, $56,000; and British Columbia almost $100,000. Those figures are amazing to me. Perhaps it will come out more clearly when I give the table which is found on page 12. This is a table on service and support of city libraries by geographic areas. The table is given in expenditure per capita. I would have you note, sir, that it is not in dollars, but in cents. The expenditure per capita on libraries in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick combined is 28 cents; on public libraries, in the province of Ontario, $1.03. Then we come to the prairie provinces and we find that it averages 90 cents. As I say, I am not bringing these out for any invidious comparison as between provinces, but generally to show the condition all across the country, a condition of which I am not particularly proud.
We are on the eve of, if we are not already in, a great period of expansion, a period in which more leisure may be anticipated. It

National Library
is a fact that our working hours are shorter. We have a five-day week in many places; we have a clear week end; and there is one thing we need to learn, if we need to learn anything: we need to learn how to use our leisure time properly, how to spend it. As one solution to that problem we should put books in the hands of the people. Classical and standard works should be available, not just in some places, not just in cities, but everywhere. At the moment there is a deplorable lack of facilities for reading.
At this point I would give another example and, again, I must go to one of the maritime provinces. I do not recall the name of the town-and, even if I did, perhaps I would not give it; because I have discovered in the house that one is likely to get into difficulties with members representing the places named. However, I do recall that the town in question was on the bank of a river-and I believe it was either in or not far from the constituency represented by the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters).
I was there one Friday evening and on the following Saturday morning had some time to spend. With the time available, I took a walk around the town. I would have said, looking at that town, that perhaps it was one of the most prosperous in Canada. There was an excellent high school, and it occurred to me that on a Saturday morning I would meet large numbers of children returning from the public library with great bundles of books in their arms-just as I see them coming from our own public library, and its various branches, in Saskatoon.
I did not see any of that. I met an old gentleman on the street and said, "Could you direct me to the public library?" He looked at me in astonishment and said, "We have no public library here." In conversation with him I said, "What do you do when you want to read? You must find it expensive to buy all your own books at present prices." He said, "I assure you we have no reading facilities here." He did point out to me that a group of ladies-I believe it was the I.O.D.E.-had a few books in their clubroom for the use of their members, but apart from that there were no other reading facilities. I have never forgotten that little experience.
It was the experience I had in that town that prompted my search for the statistics I have just placed on record. Then, if we are to have a national library, as well as efficient branches throughout the country to co-operate with it, we must have more and better trained librarians. I do not know what the experience has been in the different provinces, but I know in my own province we
[Mr. Knight.l
grant scholarships to send young people east to learn to be librarians. But that is only a drop in the bucket.
Then, we have travelling libraries serving the scattered rural areas. In the pioneer days we found those most beneficial. The travelling library, set up by the provincial government, may establish a local branch in a store or some other place that would be handy for those people wishing to borrow books. I think it is part of the responsibility of the government to see that there is a wide dissemination of books. I believe it is the responsibility of any government to encourage the cultivation of public tastes. I have no doubt there will be disagreement with that statement. I may be told that this is a free enterprise business, that there is no demand for books, that they will not find their way to the market, and so on. With that in mind I shall be content to let the statement go as I have made it.
The people of Canada find difficulty in obtaining books. I know that, because I have lived in country places and have known a total absence of books. In some places the only reading material available is a weekly newspaper; there is not even a daily paper. Then, there may be a dozen or so books to be found in the little country school library.
In this respect there is a remarkable difference between Canada and Britain. Everywhere one goes in Britain he will find book stores. That is one of the most noticeable features. There are book stores everywhere, in every little town-book stores handling secondhand books, and those handling new books. There are available first-class cheap editions of classical and standard works, which used to sell for sixpence, but would now sell for perhaps a shilling. For the expenditure of that sum one can get good reading material.
We have now made in Canada a beginning in literature and the arts. We are the heirs of those who have gone before us, of the thousands of years in the development of civilization. For the creation of things now and in the future we are dependent upon those of the past. Even original creators must have those things available to them as a basis for their ideas. That is true of the expression of ideas by the great minds of our time and of all preceding times.
As my leader has said, I believe there should be freedom in reading. With him, I am concerned about censorship, and particularly political censorship. Were it not for the youth of the country, and those for whose choice of reading material we are responsible, I would be inclined to say that, outside the provisions of the Criminal Code, there should

be no censorship at all. 1 realize that in this respect there is a problem, and that in some cases we are dealing with people whose judgment is immature.
Generally speaking, however, I would like to see the table set with a generous diet of all types of literary food; and I have enough confidence in the good sense of the Canadian people to believe that they will pick those things for their intellectual nourishment rather than those which would be injurious.
The mind must be free; the intellect must be free. The adult at least must have liberty of choice in his literary diet, so that he may choose those things which are good for him. No one, least of all some customs officer, should be able to prescribe the things the citizen shall or shall not read. I have said the need for books in Canada is great and that books are the greatest concern in national education. They are only the Cinderellas among its agencies. They have not the glamour of the radio or of the comic strip or of the movies, or the potentialities of television. Books must be made available; they must be on the shelves, and should be there in cheap editions. They should be in the public libraries of every town, of every hamlet and of every village across this country.
Yes, the need for libraries is great. They deserve all the support the government can give them, and the support and co-operation about which the Prime Minister spoke this afternoon which may be accorded to them by the national library. I would like a measure of federal aid to the humanities in somewhat the same proportion as it is being given to science. Education through books is the common concern of all parts of this nation; for the stature of the nation will ultimately be determined by the physical, spiritual and intellectual well-being of its citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I shall have a few questions to ask but, without making a speech at this time, I shall ask them in committee.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to express personally and on behalf of the government, and I think also on behalf of the people of Canada, appreciation of the attitude taken by the leaders of the different parties in the house, and those for whom they speak, in regard to this resolution which has for its purpose the establishment of a national library for the Canadian people.

I must admit that before I heard the statement of the Prime Minister and the discussion I was critical of the resolution for two reasons. In the first place I was critical because of the amount of money it would take from the taxpayers. However, the leader of the opposition and the leaders of the other groups have not said a word about extravagance; therefore it must be all right, and that satisfies me. In the second place I thought there would be some overlapping. In Ottawa we have the parliamentary library, the public library and certain other libraries, but the Prime Minister has indicated that there is to be a national library and that there will be distributing centres-if I am wrong I should like to be corrected-in Vancouver, Winnipeg and Fort William, let us say. Will these books be made available free of postage to those who want to become acquainted with Canadian affairs? I do think that the national library will provide an opportunity to sell Canada to Canadian citizens, and I think that is one of the glaring needs today. Our citizens want to know about the greatness of our land. High school teachers and university professors will welcome this library.
