speechtext: I am not able to give the hon. member the assurance that no postage stamps will be required on correspondence with the national librarian, but I am sure experience will show what is the best manner in the interests of the greatest number to make the national library of service to the development of our pride in Canadian citizenship, and that whatever experience shows to be desirable will be considered at the appropriate time in order to make the library fulfil the purpose for which it is intended.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There are a few questions I should like to ask the Prime Minister. They are based on complete support of the proposal for a national library, support which has been expressed already by all those who have spoken on the resolution. First of all I should like to ask a question or two relating to the matter of the building itself. I listened with interest to what the Prime Minister had to say, which was of course based very largely on what is set out in the Massey report and in the progress report of the national library advisory committee. We are all interested in the suggested site for the building, and it does seem to have a number of points in its favour. In fact the national library advisory committee in discussing the matter says that it has come across only one objection to the proposal, namely that it would do away with a certain amount of parking space available there at the present time, but the committee

National Library
immediately points out that even that problem could be solved in a way that the committee suggests.
We are all conscious of the problem that arises in connection with any building project at the present time because of the shortage of steel and other building materials. But I should like to emphasize the fact that the national library advisory committee in its progress report and recommendations made in November, 1951, did pronounce rather strongly on this matter. I point out that this report was made after the Massey report, and it was made in the light of present conditions. Recommendation No. 3 reads:
In order that the national library proper may be able to function effectively at the earliest possible moment, three steps should be taken without delay:
A site for the national library building should he chosen, and the committee recommends strongly that the building be placed on the bank of the Ottawa river, immediately to the west of parliament hill.
An architect should be appointed to design the building.
Construction of the library, or of a first unit, should be begun as soon as is consistent with the needs of the defence program.
The question I should like to put to the Prime Minister is whether the legislation forecast by this resolution provides authority to go ahead with the selection of the site, the appointment of an architect and perchance the construction of the building itself. Would further legislation be required for these steps or can these steps be taken under the legislation now proposed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The legislation now proposed would give authority to go ahead when parliament will have appropriated funds. The only further requirement would be a vote by parliament of the funds required to carry out projects for which there would be authority to make proposals to parliament in the present legislation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I take it the statement of the Prime Minister that the government accepts the progress report and recommendations of the national library advisory committee means that the government is in sympathy with the views expressed as to the desirability of proceeding with the building as soon as possible.

That is quite true. I thought I had emphasized that in expressing my concern, which I am sure is that of all those who know the facts, about the safety of the valuable records that we already have. I think it would be very desirable just as soon as it can be arranged to have safer storage quarters for those things that could not be replaced if we were so unfortunate as to lose them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: My next question relates to something the Prime Minister spoke about earlier. He referred to recommendations both in the Massey report and in the national library advisory committee's report that the library should provide certain services such as microfilming, duplicating books where necessary, getting copies of them in from other parts of the country and so on. What I should like to know is whether this legislation will cover all these various services. My reason for raising the question is because of the wording of the resolution which says in part that there is to be "a special account to which shall be credited any money appropriated by parliament for the purpose of acquiring books." I should like to know whether that fund can be used for these other purposes and services to which the Prime Minister referred, or is it contemplated that they will be taken care of in some other way?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Of course there is nothing very definite about it, but it is contemplated at the present time that there might be votes by parliament for the acquisition of books and that those votes should not lapse at the end of the fiscal year but should be like the votes that are made for the acquisition of pictures by the national gallery. If a vote is made for the national gallery for the purpose of acquiring pictures or objects of art it does not lapse. It is available until it has been expended, but the ordinary normal administration expenses are provided for each year by a special vote.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: My next question relates to the recommendation of the Massey commission that the present national library advisory committee should be reconstituted as a board of trustees. I note that the resolution indicates, and the Prime Minister did likewise when he spoke, that rather than a board of trustees, and rather than an advisory committee, we are to have an advisory council. I realize that the Prime Minister did comment on this. For example, he referred to the situation with respect to the national gallery as compared to the national library. Would he comment further on why the government decided to have an advisory council rather than a board of trustees as recommended by the Massey commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is intended to take care of the experimental stage. The Massey commission recommended that ultimately there be two separate organizations for the national library and the archives, but that provisionally it might be better to have the two administrations under the same head. The government accepts that recommendation. The archives, the library of parliament,

the library of the national research council and those of various departments will be called upon during the organizational stage to contribute to the establishment of the national library. It was felt that during that period it would be more desirable to have it part of the civil service of the Canadian government rather than to have a board of trustees for the national library at a time when a large portion of the organizational work would be done through agencies of the civil service which exist already.
It may be that when the set-up has been completed it will be found desirable to have it under a board of trustees, but it was felt that for the organizational period it would be better to keep it part of the ordinary civil service under the direction of the gentleman who is now the archivist and who is most competent as such. We think he would be most competent too to direct the organiza'-tional work of the national library.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is it the intention to appoint as members of this advisory council the same persons who are now members of the national library advisory committee?
No consideration has been given to the personnel of the advisory council beyond the fact that it was felt that the two librarians of parliament should be members of that advisory council.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I hope it will not hurt her chances if I recommend that you keep the person who has represented Manitoba. Miss Elizabeth Dafoe is a most competent person in this field.
What steps are being taken to carry out the recommendations of the Massey commission with respect to rearranging things in our own library of parliament? I have in mind the specific recommendation that the books and works there might be divided into two groups. There is one group of books and works that are referred to more regularly and then there is a large group of books and material which are not looked at very often but which are kept there because of their value and for safekeeping. I realize that when the whole program is carried out eventually that problem can be dealt with, but I was wondering if there is any plan to deal with it in the immediate future so that even now the library of parliament may work along the lines suggested by the Massey report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, the only planning that has been done at the present time has been to have this union catalogue completed at the earliest possible moment. That will be
National Library
most helpful in determining the place where books belonging to the Canadian people through the Canadian government should be placed. When there has been a cataloguing of those books and sufficient stack space has been provided it will be a matter for the librarian and the advisory council to determine where it will be most convenient to have these books kept.
There is no doubt that there are too many books in the library of parliament for convenient access and the proper carrying out of the work of the librarians and their assistants. At least two-thirds of those books should be kept elsewhere. A selection will have to be made. That selection will be made in the knowledge revealed by this cataloguing of all books belonging to the people and now distributed throughout the several government offices.

The Prime Minister may have dealt with the matter I have in mind during the short time I was out of the chamber when he was speaking, but I should like to ask what provision is being made for the safekeeping and preservation of information in the way of recordings both on records and film. In recent times this information has assumed a significance that never was thought of a few years ago. Many of these sound films and recordings will have a historical value in the years to come and they will have to be stored somewhere. Perhaps as years go by there will be an even greater volume of this type of information which will form part of our history of today in the days of tomorrow.
Over the week end I listened to a recording of the life of the present Queen Elizabeth which in my opinion was one of the finest of its kind, both from a historical standpoint and from the point of view of current history. I am wondering if attention has been drawn to the importance of the matters I have mentioned and what is proposed to be done about it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Up to the present time all sound recordings have been kept by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. They have at the originating studios a large number of recordings. I have not looked at them recently, but I know they have a system of cataloguing because when I have applied for certain recordings it never took them very long to tell me where they were. With regard to sound films, the film board has a catalogue of everything that it is keeping as part of its accumulation of treasures. It may well be that the time will come when certain of these things will not be looked upon as current, and will be housed merely for
23S8

National Library
safekeeping in some kind of structure that will protect them against destruction from one cause or another.
I know that not very many months ago, in connection with the film board, we were very much concerned over the danger of the destruction of some films and the danger of fires or explosions resulting from the accumulation of these films at the film board studios in Ottawa. Premises were secured in a remote area where provision was made for the proper storage of the films, to protect them and to avoid having them be a source of danger to their surroundings. No doubt that is a matter which will have to be dealt with some day, because we cannot go on accumulating films in the operating studios which are not apt to be referred to at all frequently. In this legislation no provision is being made for anything but writings and books and the like. The other matter will no doubt press forward for consideration as time goes on. We have had to provide storage facilities for films because there is a danger of their being destroyed and they are, themselves, dangerous after a certain period unless they are properly cared for.

In connection with the
national library when it is finally established and in operation, will it be working in conjunction or in collaboration with any of the other libraries across Canada? If so, what will be the degree of co-operation that may be expected between the central library and other libraries?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Their relations will be on a contractual basis, and a contract requires at least two parties to make it. Their relations will be the result of a contractual arrangement between them, and the only thing I had in mind was the illustration I gave about the exchange system that has been developed between the university of British Columbia and three or four universities in the United States. They have a union catalogue, and if someone in Vancouver wants something that is not available in the library of that university but is available in one of the associated libraries, the librarian of the university communicates with the library where the book is to be found. It is sent to Vancouver on the responsibility of the university of British Columbia, and there the librarian makes it available in the manner he feels fitting to the person who wants to consult it. In some cases that person is not allowed to remove the book from the reading rooms of the library, and in another case it can be removed as if it were a book belonging to the library of the university.

There is also frequent recourse to this procedure: instead of sending the book a microfilm is made of the pages or material that is required and the microfilm is sent. The intention is to have this developed by expert technicians, making use of the experience of others, to establish and operate a system that will make the organization as beneficial to as many as possible.

Will the Prime Minister
indicate in a very general way at this stage of the resolution just what this is going to cost us? Would he indicate how much the building is going to cost and how much the general administration is going to cost?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I cannot indicate how much the building is going to cost because building costs are not very stable at the present time; and I cannot indicate when the building is going to be started, nor even what its dimensions are apt to be. The pattern is very apt to be the same as has been followed by the national gallery. If the hon. gentleman will get a copy of this booklet which is available, "The National Gallery of Canada Competition", he will see how the board of governors of the national gallery is proceeding with that competition to choose an architect, and what is apt to follow the selection of the architect.
With respect to the increase in expenditures over what is provided for in the estimates which are before the house, the estimate for the bibliographical service now is $48,109, and that is to carry on the same work as has been going on for the last two years. The actual expenditure for 1950-51 was $30,339; in 195152, it was $37,151. Dr. Lamb estimates that the additional work for a full year might amount to something of the order of $60,000, making about $108,000 in all. That would be the expenditure that would be incurred for the organizational work until we get around to the point of either purchasing new books or putting up a new building; that would be for the completion of the work required to publish this union catalogue, which it is hoped to complete within five years; to add to this "Canadiana" which is now being published monthly, other departments making it a full fledged national bibliography, and to organize the first unit of the cataloguing department of the national library proper in order that work may start on the task of cataloguing the thousands of books now under the supreme court building and elsewhere. The additional expense that is apt to be required for the current fiscal year might be of the order of $50,000 or $60,000.
Very respectfully, I wonder if no estimate has been made whatever of what this project is going to cost the taxpayers; that is what I should like to get at.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, no estimate has been made of what this project will cost the taxpayer. It is felt that it will not cost the taxpayer more than its intrinsic, monetary value, and that its developmental value for the Canadian people will be beyond its intrinsic monetary value or cost.

I agree that probably it will. But it seems strange that the government of Canada should come before parliament asking for a project and not give us some idea of what the cost is going to be. I should like to be respectful but may I at the same time ask this question: Is this going to be another project-like, for instance, the Prime Minister's house-where we start out, keep adding and adding, and do not know where we are going? I think an estimate should be made. I do not see why it should be difficult for it to be made.

Mr. Chairman, when there is the prospect of going ahead with the work an estimate will be prepared and there will be a request to parliament to vote the money. If the hon. member is here at that time, he can criticize it and vote against it if he thinks it is extravagant.

As a matter of information, may I ask the Prime Minister how many books there are now in the present library of parliament? Perhaps the Prime Minister did not come prepared to give that information; but if he has it, we should like it to be given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should not like to be positive about that figure. At the present time about 2 million books are listed in what has been done so far on the union catalogue, most of those books being in libraries in Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal. I do not know how many belong to the Canadian people and how many belong to the other libraries of the number that are comprised in this figure of 2 million that have already been catalogued.

If the Prime Minister can get the information, perhaps he might give it to the committee some time. It is a matter of some interest. Those who go through the library from time to time ask how big the library is and how many books are in it. This information would, I think, satisfy the curiosity of the members of the house. There is a wide area covered by the books that are in the library. As the Prime Minister knows, they go all the way from children's books to books on Einstein's theory of relativity. That
National Library
illustration shows the extent of the fields they cover. I had occasion to find that fact out for myself through a rather interesting experience some years ago when one of the junior members of our family was down here and found herself in the library taking out a book which satisfied her extent of learning. Some six months later I was amazed to be billed for the book. The communication I received stated that Mr. Graydon had taken out a volume entitled "The Bobbsey Twins in Toyland" and that I ought to return it at once. I therefore have occasion to speak with some measure of personal experience with regard to the capacity of the library to satisfy readers of all ages.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) mentioned about three-quarters of a million books. I think that figure is somewhat exaggerated. The figure I get from Dr. Lamb is that there are about 550,000 books in the library of parliament. The other information I had was that the cataloguing that has been done thus far comprises something over 2 million books in Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto, which it is hoped by this system to make available. There may be quite a lot of duplication in the 2 million volumes that have been catalogued but the effort will be to avoid unnecessary duplication. There are, of course, some books that it will be desirable to have in all these libraries; but there are others the presence of which in one library may be sufficient for the needs of those who apply to libraries elsewhere.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a number of references have been made this afternoon to the large number of books in the parliamentary library and to the difficulty that confronts any of us who go there if we try to find certain books ourselves. Nevertheless, I think a tribute should be paid to the staff of that library for the efficient service they give us. They seem to be able to find almost any book we can possibly ask for, and they are able to dig it out quite readily. The service is of the best, but even so, I am sure we all agree that the facilities, for their sake and ours, should be greatly improved.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Peel and the Prime Minister were discussing the question of films and recordings of one kind or another. I noted that the Prime Minister's reply was to the effect that at the moment it is not contemplated that the national library collection should go beyond books and similar items. I should like to draw to the attention of the Prime Minister the fact that this question was discussed in the Massey report. On pages 104 and 105 there is a record of the representations made

National Library
to the commission on these matters. Then there is a recommendation over on page 332 of the Massey report. In the earlier part of the volume it is pointed out that representations were made that the national library might be a depository for, amongst other things, maps, music, art, photographs, films and recordings. When one hears art mentioned, he realizes that is something that would seem to be better in the national gallery. But at page 332 of its report, the Massey commission made this recommendation:
That the board of trustees be empowered to add to its collection Canadian music, in printed or manuscript form, and such records, films and photographs as are considered necessary supplements to the printed collection of books, pamphlets and newspapers ...
And so on. I do not press it as an argument at this time, but I think it should be on the record at this point. I trust that the authorities will bear in mind this recommendation when the national library is being set up. Indeed, if it is recognized that one of the functions of the national library is to be that of a repository not only of material that is referred to day by day but of items that tell the story of Canada across the years, it would seem that items of this other kind should be there along with books and similar documents.
I wish to say one other word, Mr. Chairman. I make this suggestion on behalf of my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who had to leave the chamber in order to attend another meeting; it is in connection with the building itself. We all understand that the motion before us does not provide for the erection of a building. In answer to a question of mine earlier, the Prime Minister made it clear that authority will be provided by this resolution to look into the question of the site, the engaging of an architect and the collecting of designs. I express the hope -and in doing so I support the recommendation of the national library advisory committee and others-that as little time as possible will be lost in proceeding with the project of the building itself. The national library will not be a reality until we have a building. Let us hope it can be erected soon. *
The suggestion that my leader was anxious to make, had he been able to stay, was to the effect that consideration be given, when the plans for the building are in contemplation, to both the artistic and the functional aspects of modern architecture. There are libraries that go in for the artistic type, and there are libraries which are designed on functional lines; there are many of the latter in the world today. It would seem that there is room for both considerations. We hope

attention will be given to both of those aspects when the time comes-and we hope that time is not far off-to consider the project of the building itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Canada Grain Act to provide for the reappointment of grain commissioners and for increases in their salaries; to provide also for the appointment and salaries of three assistant grain commissioners instead of four; and to provide further for certain technical amendments of the statutory grades of grain.
Will the minister be making a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes. The proposed amendments to the Canada Grain Act fall into four general categories.
The first relates to the salaries and appointments of the members of the board of grain commissioners, and of the assistant grain commissioners. The present salaries, fixed in 1930, are no longer adequate. The lack of any specific provision in the act for reappointment of the commissioners is being corrected. The number of assistant grain commissioners is being reduced from four to three.
Secondly, there is a revision relating to section 85 of the act which specifies the form in which certain records maintained by the elevator operators must be kept.
A further amendment is intended to give authority to the governor in council to issue regulations. In the act, as it is now, only the board of grain commissioners may make regulations or orders.
Finally, there are some amendments to the definitions of statutory grades which are set out in the schedules to the act.

At this time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer briefly to the work of the board of grain commissioners. Usually when wheat matters are being discussed in this house, attention is centred on particular marketing or delivery problems. Because the board's work is of a detailed and technical nature, it is very easy for the public to overlook the importance of it and the competence with which it is being done. We all speak frequently of the high reputation enjoyed by Canadian grains in the markets of the world, a reputation which is a direct result of the efficiency of the inspection and grading system administered by the board of grain commissioners. I am happy to have this opportunity to pay tribute to their work.
Referring again to the amendments which are being proposed, it should be noted that they include no amendment with respect to overages at country elevators. This question has been referred to frequently in this house, particularly during the last two sessions. Representations have been made to the government that overages arising as a result of country elevator operations should be confiscated and the proceeds distributed through the wheat board to producers. After careful consideration the government has come to the conclusion that such a proposal could lead only to greater difficulties. Moreover, it would not provide a satisfactory solution for the individual farmer who feels that he has special ground for complaint. All that such a farmer would receive by way of recompense would be a minute addition to his participation payment.
The record shows that, year in and year out, shortages or overages are an extremely small fraction of the total quantities of grain handled. In a return tabled in the house recently it was shown that during the crop year 1950-51 gross overages of all country elevators were only -08 of 1 per cent of total quantities received at country elevators and net overages were only -28 of 1 per cent. Under the exceptional conditions of the preceding five years the net overage for wheat was -24 of 1 per cent. Some elevator houses, of course, experienced shortages.
In the light of all the information it has had available, the government has not felt justified, without having the soundness of such a course much more clearly established, in putting forward an amendment which would carry out the recommendation that country elevator overages should be confiscated and delivered to the wheat board. The matter of finding the best solution of this problem is a difficult one, and I hope it will be given thorough study in the agriculture committee.
Canada Grain Act
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that it is my intention to recommend that the bill which will be based on this resolution, after it has obtained second reading, be sent to the agriculture committee for study.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to hear the minister announce that the bill will be referred to the agriculture committee for study. I think that should reduce considerably the comment at this particular stage.
The duties of the board of grain commissioners are very important. They have a heavy task. I was also glad to hear the minister pay a tribute to the commissioners for the very onerous work they have had to perform in the past. Many people in this country do not realize what the duties of the grain commissioners really are. In fact many grain producers get the grain commissioners mixed up with the wheat board, whose functions are very different. For example, the board of grain commissioners are responsible for the grading of grain; the weighing of any grain; the deductions made from any grain for dockage or shrinkage; any shortage appearing upon the delivery of any grain into or out of any elevator; the unfair or discriminatory operation of any elevator; the deterioration of any grain during storage or shipment; the refusal or neglect of any person to comply with any provisions of the act or of any regulation made or licence issued pursuant thereto. Then they are also responsible to some extent for the transportation of grain and the allocation of cars and so forth.
When the matter is referred to the committee on agriculture for further study, I would hope that some of the officials responsible for grading, and even the chief chemist, might be available for questioning before the committee. I say that because some doubt has arisen as to whether the weather conditions of the past couple of years or anything else have been responsible for difficulties in grading. There is some doubt in the prairie provinces as to whether we have the best system of grading wheat and cereals in this country. Just across the border in the United States their wheat is graded, I think, more on the protein content than in this country. Therefore I think it will be very useful if the minister or his proper officials would arrange to have Dr. Anderson, I think it is, the chief chemist of the board of grain commissioners, and such officials as that available for questioning before the committee, because it certainly would be very instructional to the members and to the producers of wheat back home who have a very vague understanding, and in some cases a misunderstanding, of this whole undertaking.

Canada Grain Act
Since the measure is to be referred to the committee I do not wish to take up any further time. I hope the minister will make these officials available to the committee so we can obtain information and try to come to an understanding as to whether we really have the best system of grading grain at the present time in Canada. It is a very vexed question, and X hope that will be done.

I should like to say a very few words at this stage of the proceedings. I am glad the minister is having this bill referred to the agriculture committee, and also the annual report of -the board of grain commissioners, where they can be discussed and we can get further evidence. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) with regard to having certain officials of the board before the committee is very good. The board of grain commissioners for years have had the reputation of being the watchdog of the farmers' interests in the grain trade. Sometimes I think, particularly during the last few years, they have lost contact with the farmers. Just whose fault that is, I do not know. I think sometimes the duties of the board should be given more publicity by the board itself, so that they may keep that direct contact with the farmer.
The result of this is that there has been considerable criticism of the board in the last two or three years with respect to the matter of overages, and certain other matters. The minister has stated that the government have considered the representations made to them with respect to overages and decided that no further amendments should be made in this matter. I suggest that before he closes his mind on the subject some of the farm representatives should be heard before the committee on agriculture. I do not think any harm could be done by that. If they have a case, well and good; if they have not, then the committee on agriculture would: be able to listen to their evidence and to the evidence given by the handling firms in the trade, and come to some conclusion in the matter.
The present amendments are not major amendments. I think through the years we have to take the Canada Grain Act at certain intervals, and go over it to see that it is up to date and in line with our present methods of handling crops in western Canada. There has been a revolution in the last ten years in the marketing and handling of western grain. The combine has displaced the old threshing machine, and trucks have displaced the wagon in which, grain used to be delivered. Today crops are handled much faster and under conditions quite different from what they were ten or fifteen years

ago. This has created problems, and those problems can be ironed out only through consultation with farm, organizations and handling firms. That is why I think we should have a thorough discussion of this whole grain handling question before the committee on agriculture.
The matter of the car order book has been to the front in western Canada. The controller has discontinued the use of that book, and he may have very good reasons for doing so. In western Canada, however, there has been criticism of this procedure, and I think we should hear representatives of farm organizations before the minister comes to any firm decision. Witnesses should be called from handling firms and farm organizations in western Canada. If out of that discussion come some further amendments which the committee believes should be included, then they should be placed in this measure before it is returned to the house.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to support the resolution, and I am also pleased that the minister proposes to refer the matter to the committee on agriculture. As was stated by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), I hope the agricultural organizations will be permitted: to make their submissions to the committee. When the matter is being dealt with I hope the minister will allow a full discussion of matters connected with the Canada Grain Act, and that we will not be tied down to a discussion of only the amendments in the measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not think I could, even if I tried,

I am glad to have that assurance. I realize the question of overages is a difficult one. On the other hand I am sorry there is no amendment proposed to deal with the matter. I have always felt that to a large extent the solution lies within the hands of the farmers. They sell their grain to the pool elevators, and the benefits of the sales of overages come back to them in participation dividends.
I realize, of course, that it is not possible for all farmers to sell grain to the pool elevators, because if all grain were held there we would find congestion. I have always sold to the pool elevators, and the question of overages has never worried me because I feel I will get back any adjustment there may be, or at least my proportion of it, when the participation dividends are paid.
As I am a member of the committee, I shall not say more at this time.

Mr. Speaker, with other members I welcome the minister's announcement that this bill will be sent to the committee on agriculture. speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 225, to incorporate the Hotel Mutual Insurance Company.

Would the sponsor explain the bill?
Private Bills

The purpose of the bill is the incorporation of the Hotel Mutual Insurance Company by a group of Albertans, namely Douglas Earl George, bank manager, of Edson, Alberta; and Eugene Pechet, hotel proprietor and Russell Driscoll, barrister, both of the city of Edmonton. These three men are the provisional directors. After the formation of the company a board of directors will be elected consisting of not less than nine and not more than twenty-one members. The capital stock of the proposed company will be $3 million of which $250,000 shall have been subscribed before the general meeting is called. Business may be commenced only after $500,000 of the capital stock has been subscribed and $300,000 paid thereon.
Section 6 of the bill sets out twenty-six classes of insurance for which the company may make contracts. Section 7, however, lists the types of contracts in which the insurance company is immediately interested. The company will operate under the general rules and provisions of the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932. As the name of the company would indicate, its main purpose is to insure hotels. However, it is to be both a mutual and a stockholders' company. The policyholders as well as the shareholders will participate in the profits. Persons who buy a policy of not less than $5,000 will be entitled to attend the annuel meeting and vote for the election of directors.
This bill has had first and second readings in the Senate, has passed the Senate committee, has been given third, reading in the Senate, and is now referred to this house. The bill has the complete approval of the superintendent of insurance. It is my hope that after second reading the bill will be referred to the House of Commons standing committee on banking and commerce.

On the night of May 16 when this bill was last before the house I had considered it advisable in the interests of all concerned to say something as regards the stability of the oil industry in Alberta so that all those interested might be able to form some sort of estimate with respect to

Boundary Pipeline Corporation whether the industry is a fly-by-night affair. I presented some evidence to show that the Alberta oil development is not a windfall but that it has taken place as the result of very careful, wise and prudent planning based upon fundamental principles which have been laid down as a consequence of the most thoroughgoing inquiry and study, and which have been adhered to religiously. They are principles to which the Social Credit administration now in power in Alberta is committed. It committed itself definitely in a statement by Hon. N. E. Tanner, minister of lands and mines at the time in the Social Credit government, who probably more than any other one man in Canada was responsible for the drafting and laying down of the policy and the administration thereof as a result of which the spectacular development of the oil industry in Alberta has taken place.
From a statement made by Mr. Tanner to the people of Alberta in 1948 I had read the five fundamental principles upon which the policy for the development and maintenance of the Alberta oil industry was established- and was to be maintained. I think it well to give a few more details along the same line I followed the other night.
Referring once more to the question whether the Alberta oil development was a windfall,
I might liken it to an irrigation district. After an irrigation project is thoroughly established and in operation it may be said that it was a windfall. It is true it was a windfall in so far as the fact that the water was there, the land was there and money was spent to develop the irrigation canals, distribution ditches and all the other things; but to say it was a windfall would give an altogether wrong impression as to the part played in the development of it by the men whose responsibility it was to bring about that development. Therefore I think we are safe in saying that the Alberta government earned the oil development just as thoroughly as the group of men in charge of the irrigation project earned that project by doing the work and spending the money involved in developing it.
I had begun to refer to the question of private enterprise. The Alberta people believe in private enterprise. Social Credit believes in private enterprise. Social Credit believes that public ownership of industry in a general way is a false principle and that it is not in the best interests of any economy. It is largely as a result of the attitude of the Alberta people and the Social Credit government in this respect that those with great sums of money to invest in the development of oil have been encouraged to come to Alberta, spend the great amount of money they have spent and remain there to proceed

Boundary Pipeline Corporation rises according to the time of year. There is no deviation from the principle which I have laid down.

It must be borne in mind that a considerable amount of Alberta's oil-producing land was alienated from the province before the natural resources of the province were given to it in 1932. In former times, even before 1905, the federal government at Ottawa was in a position to alienate this land. Some of the land would1 naturally be in the hands of the Hudson's Bay Company, some in the hands of the Canadian Pacific and some in the hands of the C. and E. Corporation. Where oil was found on property belonging to any of these people possessing a prior right, it is not under the same regulations as are the lands which belong to the province. Is that clear?

The next important matter in which I think nearly everyone is interested, and which I believe has a bearing on the general matter we are discussing tonight, is how much money has been made by the province as a result of these oil developments. Some people act as though they thought something like billions had fallen down in a cloudburst of financial returns, but no such thing is true. Those are only rainbow dreams. I give these figures, not only for the sake of those who desire to know about that, but to show the rate at which the oil industry has developed, thereby indicating the possible development for the future.
Alberta received in revenue from oil in 1948-49, $10,340,000. That was the first year after the amazing development took place following the discovery of the oil in the famous Leduc field. In 1949-50 she received $26,550,000; in 1950-51, $32,768,000; in 1951-52, to December 31, 1951, $20,262,000. Those figures will be found in Premier Manning's 1952 budget speech. This indicates that no such unbelievable streams of money flowed from the oil industry. The estimate for 195253 is $38,300,000, which will include $12 million from crown reserves and $10,300,000 from oil royalties, $12,500,000 from fees and oil lease rentals. For the facts pertinent to these statements we can refer to Premier Manning's 1952 budget speech, and those who want to read it can find it in the Lethbridge Herald of March 8, pages 1 and 19, which can be found in our reading room. These facts show that all those who attribute the whole of Alberta's financial success to the oil industry are just a little wide of the mark.
It is important to bear In mind, summing up in a general way, that thus far the Alberta Social Credit government did everything it could to help those who came to develop her oil industry, realizing the value of the companies who came in and not making it difficult for them. In the first place, the government learned all the known facts about the oil industry. Then it set up a source of information to be available to all comers, so that any company entering the field could go to the fountain of this information and get millions of dollars worth of valuable facts about the sort of thing that might be encountered, before it did a tap of prospecting or drilling. The very best experts were available at all times to give the finest advice that could be obtained.

This is one of the great things to the credit of the administration of Alberta in respect of the oil development.
I have already referred to the information that answers the question:	Is the Social
Credit government permitting the big oil companies to commit abuses? I have pointed out that "no" is the answer. No Alberta oil lands have been alienated from the crown. All development is purely on a lease basis. No monopolistic development is permitted. No special privileges are permitted. No injury to owners of the lands is permitted without compensation. It can readily be seen that if companies are allowed to go rambling all over the province drilling here, there and everywhere, spoiling men's farms, knocking down their crops and all that kind of thing without any remuneration to the property owners, in all probability the people of Alberta will become weary of that sort of thing and turn out a government that would permit it. The government has set up a right of entry arbitration board to see that farmers get fair and generous treatment where oil wells are drilled on their farms. If the oil company and the farmer cannot make a satisfactory settlement it is referred to the board for settlement.

Boundary Pipeline Corporation

Mr. Chairman, in taking part in this debate tonight, I want to assure you at the outset that I will not ask for the privilege of having my time extended beyond the forty-five minute limit.
I am opposed to this bill in the first place because the line stops at Winnipeg. The incorporation of this Boundary Pipeline company would mean that it would build a pipe line to Winnipeg. I am anxious that we receive this power in Ontario; we need it now in Ontario to develop the province. Industry here is short of power. Therefore we need this gas which belongs to Canada. We need it in the eastern section of Canada now.
In the first place, this small pipe line going to Winnipeg was intended to go to the boundary, but certain objections were taken in the committee and the applicants withdrew that part of it, and said: We will stop at Winnipeg. There is no doubt in my mind that this pipe line was meant to go to the boundary and then be taken over by some other company which would deliver gas to the different parts of the United States. I think it has been proven that throughout the years we have been the suppliers of natural resources for the large cities of the United States. That is probably one reason Sir Wilfrid Laurier's dream has not come true yet, when he said that the nineteenth century belonged to the United States but the twentieth century belongs to Canada.
If we are going to develop Canada, we must have cheap power and we have to develop our natural resources here at home. This is one potential source of power we must make use of. We can make use of it to the great benefit of this nation. I do not see the United States shipping to us over here anything they require first at home. That is probably one reason they have developed so much faster than we have over the past seventy-five years. They are a great nation and a developing neighbour. But I should like to tell this committee that the greatest asset they have is not the Atlantic ocean, the Pacific ocean or Mexico but rather this northern boundary alongside of which lies Canada which is supplying them with gold, iron ore, pulp-wood, timber, lumber and nickel which is necessary in any kind of a war, machine or defence program.
They are the best customers we have, too.

Yes, they have been good customers of ours; but this is not a oneway street. I think we should protect Canada and Canadian interests first. Do not

Boundary Pipeline Corporation forget that our large cities along the border will need this gas and this power in order to compete with the large cities that lie along the border in the United States. Are we going to go on developing those large cities of the United States, or are we going to make possible more employment and more industry in Canada?
The pipe line is to be a small one, to start with. I think it has been proven in committee-it was to me, anyway-that the potential market for what power will be used from the oil fields to Winnipeg will not warrant, financially, a pipe line of any kind, but it might have the effect of stopping the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company, which was granted a charter last year, from coming on through Ontario, Quebec and the eastern provinces, because it will absorb the market provided by all the towns and cities from the oil wells to Winnipeg. Therefore the pipe line for which we have already granted a charter, to be built right across Canada and which I think is most necessary, might not have enough market to warrant its construction for some 1,200 or 1,300 miles before it would get one customer. The first customers would be in northern Ontario, and would be such large cities as Fort William and Port Arthur.

monopoly.

We need gas in Ontario to develop hydroelectric power. We are short of electric power in Ontario. We need cheap fuel in order to generate electricity to be used in the rural districts of Ontario and Quebec. Do not forget that when you turn on a light in a home in the country you not only turn on a light in the kitchen or living room of the house, but in the heart of the housewife.
I can tell you why we are short of power in Ontario, and why we need this gas. In Ontario we have had a great hydro development going on for the last eight years. Power lines, dams and power projects have been built as fast as the Hydro Electric Power Commission could get steel, wire, cement, machinery and things to do it with. It has been a wonderful development. However, it has not caught up with the shortage of power, and it has not coped with the speed of industrial development throughout the province. I do not mind telling the committee why there is a shortage of power in Ontario. In 1934 a Liberal government came into power in this province. One of the things the premier, Mr. Hepburn, who was elected at that time, fought the election on was the building of .power

lines. He said the building of power lines and power dams was a waste of money, and that Ontario had enough power to do it for a hundred years. But he was very shortsighted because before 1940 we had caught up with all the power we had developed and needed more.

If anybody tells me that we do not need gas for cheap power in Ontario I will tell them that they do not know what they are talking about. They certainly do not know anything about eastern Canada.
That coal is coming in from the United States. Just think of the amount of foreign exchange that could be saved in Ontario if instead of buying that coal we could buy Alberta gas. Another aspect of box car distribution in western Canada that I should like to mention is this. The experience I have seen from one elevator marketing point to another is that the elevator houses themselves are filled up early in the crop year, perhaps a few days or a week after harvesting becomes general. Then when railway companies bring in box cars to the elevator points they are usually divided on an equal basis amongst the elevator companies doing business at a particular elevator
Canada Crain Act
point. On the surface such a distribution of box cars may appear fair, but I believe that at the vast majority of marketing points most farmers would like to market their grain through their own co-operative elevator system. On May 12 a return was tabled in answer to a question of mine as to the reduction in quantities of wheat, oats, barley and flax resulting from drying operations. As a result of drying, I would say from quick calculation that the reduction was some one and a quarter million bushels. A part of the answer to my question reads as follows:
No reduction or loss in weight occurs in the natural drying process whereby tough and/or damp grades are dried by mixing with grain of straight grade.

Elevator book stocks are adjusted tor any drying loss through the cancellation of warehouse receipts covering the quantities of tough and damp grain to be dried, and by the registration of new warehouse receipts for the amount of the dried grain in accordance with the board's regulation No. 15, section 6 (g).
If at all possible I believe that kind of information should be placed in the annual report. I do not know whether or not it is in that report, since it has not been printed and distributed, but I believe that is the kind of information the prairie producers would like to obtain.
There is one other matter I should like to raise at this time, the question of introducing a protein factor into the grading system for wheat. As the minister knows, over the years farmers, particularly in the drier sections of western Canada, have advocated the grading of wheat on a protein basis. I have noticed that the chief chemist of the board of grain commissioners, Dr. J. A. Anderson, has given a good deal of thought and study to this problem. Reports have appeared in the press from time to time with respect to papers he has delivered to meetings of various farm organizations. I think he has done a service to western Canada by the study he has made of a protein grading system. It is his opinion that a protein factor introduced into the grading of wheat would be advantageous to western wheat producers in that it would likely result in a greater economic return for wheat.
He outlines the way such a protein factor could be introduced into a grading system for wheat. He goes on to explain that there is no quick method of ascertaining the amount of protein in any given sample of wheat, and because there is no quick way of obtaining the protein content it is difficult to grade

wheat on a protein basis when the wheat must be moved quickly to marketing positions. Dr. Anderson goes on to point out that a study is being made of possible methods to quickly determine the protein content of wheat. I hope that the minister, the national research council and other government departments have been working with Dr. Anderson and giving him every assistance possible so that a mechanical device to rapidly determine the protein content of wheat may finally be invented. From Dr. Anderson's comments apparently that is the only major hurdle that needs to be overcome to place the grading of wheat on a protein factor basis.
As I have said, he points out that such a protein grading system would increase the economic return to western producers, would probably be more satisfactory for most milling companies in Canada, and should result in Canadian wheat obtaining a somewhat better price on the world's markets. For this reason I hope Dr. Anderson will be given every encouragement and assistance in his very valuable work.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minister of Transport) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ZONING OF AIRPORTS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 194, to amend the Aeronautics Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to provide for airport zoning. I will now endeavour to deal at some length with the principles embodied in this measure.
Airport zoning consists of the promulgation of comprehensive zoning regulations dividing the area surrounding an airport into zones, specifying the uses of the land permitted in these zones, and regulating and restricting the height of structures and trees. The parliament of Canada having exclusive jurisdiction over air navigation and airports, it appears that enabling legislation of this parliament is required in order to deal with this pressing problem.
The bill to amend the Aeronautics Act may be considered under two heads. The first deals with the authority for making zoning regulations and the second with the procedure to be followed and the payment of

compensation in respect of property injuriously affected by the application of the regulations.
The layman is apt to think that an airport consists solely of its material features, its runways, taxiways, loading areas, lighting equipment, buildings and other facilities. But all of these would be of little practical value if the airport did not have adequate aerial approaches. Aircraft ascend and descend at a very gradual rate. A clear slope must be allowed for in approaching the field and in departing from it. Moreover, the clearance must not be such that the planes will just scrape over the tops of obstacles. The margin allowed should be such that normal landings and take-offs may be made with the planes always some distance above the tops of buildings, power lines, trees and other obstacles.
It must be evident that the effective size of an airport is determined as much by its surroundings as by its own ground area. The erection of buildings and other structures in the vicinity of an airport which are an obstruction to aircraft using the airport would threaten and perhaps destroy the utility of the airport and the large investment of public funds it might represent. But this is by no means the only or most serious consequence of such obstruction of an airport approaches. Of even greater concern is the fact that an approach obstruction endangers the lives and property of flyers and their passengers as well as those of occupants of land in the vicinity. Obstructed approaches are the cause of many aeroplane crashes and a contributing factor in a great number of others.
The problem presented by this necessity for clear aircraft approaches is not only one of removing, lowering, marking and lighting existing airport hazards but one of preventing the establishment or creation of additional hazards. Unless ways are found and steps taken to limit to the extent necessary the height of future buildings, transmission lines, other structures, and objects of natural growth located on property in the vicinity of an airport, it may be expected that many such structures and objects will be erected or allowed to grow to heights making them obstructions or hazards to aircraft using the airport.
Air transportation in the past few years has increased at a phenomenal rate and the future promises further expansion. Since this expansion is bound to bring with it rapid industrial or residential development of areas near airports, it will become increasingly more difficult to deal with the problem of preventing obstruction of airport approaches if the present situation is allowed to continue. The
Aeronautics Act
more airport obstructions that are permitted, the more difficult and expensive will be the task of eliminating the existing obstructions and preventing the establishment of others.
The international civil aviation organization has studied this problem and has recommended certain practices in respect of airport zoning to which Canada has subscribed and which the government proposes to follow so far as the circumstances in each case will permit. The requirements vary somewhat according to the use to which an airport is to be put and the type of aircraft that will be using it under a variety of conditions. On the major civil airports certain runways may be designated for use on instrument landing approach. The requirements in respect of these particular runways are naturally more exacting than in the case of those that are limited to the use of visual flight rules. On certain military airports the characteristics of the aircraft using them are such that severe limitations in the matter of airport zoning are necessary.
There are several methods by which airport approaches may be protected against obstructions. One is for the owner of the airport to obtain title to the property in the vicinity of the airport upon which obstructions might be erected. Any hazards already in existence could then be removed or lowered and the land retained or sold subject to restrictions limiting the height of buildings and other objects that might be constructed thereon. In the case of federal airports resort may be had to expropriation if the land owners are unwilling to sell. However, the expense involved is the principal drawback to this method of zoning as the acreage required would be many times that necessary for the airport proper.
At this point I should like to repeat what I said then when speaking on the resolution. It is not the intention of the bill to provide for the removal of existing obstructions. This will be taken care of by the normal procedures of acquiring lands or easements by purchase or expropriation. The zoning regulations contemplated by this legislation would apply to prevent the future erection of buildings or other structures which might become obstructions to aircraft.
The method of zoning by regulations as provided for in this bill is the most satisfactory solution to the problem in that it may be applied to all airports whether government, municipal or privately owned. It is the least expensive method, but at the same tSne provides for adequate compensation to property holders whose lands are injuriously affected. It avoids separate dealings with a

Aeronautics Act
multitude of property holders. Few steps are of such urgency and few steps are so essential to promote safety.
Generally, the nature of the proposed zoning regulations will follow a plan which will be somewhat as follows. From the centre of an airport a circle may be described having a radius of thirteen thousand feet. Within this circle no structure will be permitted to have an elevation above 150 feet.
In addition to this restriction, the approach flightways which commence at the end of the runways and extend outward from the bound-iary of the airport will be restricted to structures not exceeding one foot in height for every fifty feet that these structures are located from the boundary.
There will also be restrictions on the lateral slopes on each side of the flightways extending outward and upward at a ratio of one foot in height for every seven feet of horizontal distance. This is rather technical but I think it conveys the general idea of what restrictions may be expected. As each airport has different characteristics, the zoning regulations will be adapted to the plan of the individual airport.
There may also be odd cases where the use of land adjacent to an airport may have to be restricted. For instance, it would be dangerous to have machines in the vicinity of an airport which give off smoke or fumes hazardous to aircraft.
It is proposed to take immediate action, if this measure becomes law, in respect of certain airports operated by the departments of Transport and National Defence. Over a period of years it will be necessary to give this protection to all government airports. At the present time there are 114 of these, not including military airports. In due time it will also be necessary to deal with the zoning of municipal airports where the problems will have to be discussed with the municipalities concerned. There are now 17 airports on the transcontinental airways system operated by the Department of Transport which require immediate protection.
I turn now to the second part of the bill. Provision is made for adequate publication of the zoning regulations which in the case of civil airports will be made by the Minister of Transport and approved by the governor in council. The plan and description of the lands affected by a zoning regulation will be signed and deposited in the land registry office in the same way as is now the practice under the Expropriation Act. A copy of the regulation will be published in the Canada Gazette and in two successive issues of at least two newspapers serving the area where
[Mr. Chevrler.l
the airport is located. This should give sufficient publicity to the regulations.
As I have stated, the bill provides for payment of compensation in cases where property is injuriously affected by the operation of the zoning regulations. The yardstick for measuring compensation will be the amount by which the property is decreased in value by the enactment of the regulations, less the amount by which the property has increased in value after the claimant became the owner, and is attributable to the airport. This is a well known and accepted principle of compensation, and is to be found in the Exchequer Court Act where the court is directed to take into account any advantage or benefit that accrues or is likely to accrue from the construction or operation of a public work.
I have already indicated my view that in the long run owners of property in the vicinity of an airport will benefit from the orderly development of the area under a zoning plan. I recognize, however, that cases will arise where a property owner may be prevented from proceeding with plans for the development of property which will have to be altered or abandoned. In these cases claims will be dealt with by negotiation and fair settlements made. If the parties are unable to agree, the claimant has recourse to the exchequer court which will settle the compensation.
The bill provides for a time limit for making claims of one year from the date of deposit made in the land registry office. It is not proposed to pay out public moneys to claimants unless they come forward within a reasonable time to make their claims.
In the preparation of this legislation considerable study was given to action taken by the United Kingdom and the United States to meet this problem. In both these countries provision has been made by legislation for zoning airports. The physical details concerning the limitations to be imposed are based on international recommendations.
I consider this bill to be a forward step in the field of aviation. It should be enacted as a necessary protection for those who travel by air and those who dwell near airports. The development of the aviation industry in Canada is proceeding rapidly and deserves the support of all members of this house.

The minister is a distinguished member of the bar and I should think he would be the first to admit that, in all these instances, there is the odd case where a great deal of injustice might result from the too stringent application of a time limit. I think there ought to be something in the regulations which would give a judge of the exchequer court some latitude when dealing with a case where extreme hardship is shown as the result of the one year limitation.
Then I should like to deal with a matter raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), and which I wish to emphasize. I refer to the question as to how compensation is to be arrived at or adjusted. I cannot see why a court should be put in a position where it is in a strait-jacket when it comes to the manner in which it can arrive

at proper compensation. In the first place the minister indicates that the regulations will call for compensation as a result of damages flowing from the zoning regulations in the vicinity of an airport. At the same time, while he gives with one hand he takes away with the other. He indicates that consideration must be given also to the fact that, while in the hands of the owner, the properties may have increased in value by virtue of the location of the airport.
I take objection to the stand taken by the minister, and hope when the committee sits he will not be adamant in the position he has taken in this regard. I have a feeling that this restrictive portion of his regulations, which he proposes to enforce through the exchequer court, might easily have the effect of rendering an injustice to many land owners whom, normally, the court would wish to help.
I would suggest to the minister, who has given a great deal of study to this matter and who has not pressed the legislation too hastily-and I must give him full marks for that, because there has been a considerable lapse of time to give those who are interested an opportunity to come forward and make their suggestions-that these are two points to which he might give special attention. When he comes before the committee I hope he will not appear as an adamant defender of the regulations he now proposes. I would hope that he would be amenable to suggestions and would see, in the name of sweet reason and justice, just how important these two suggestions are, coming as they do from people representing those who may make claims in the future.
Like the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, who has spoken officially on behalf of the official opposition, I would hope that in having this matter placed before the committee these two changes might be made, in the interests of those who may be dealing with the government as a result of zoning regulations in the days ahead.

Mr. Speaker, may I add a brief word largely along the line of the speeches made tonight by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon).
Every member of the house of course supports the principle of ensuring as far as possible safety around our airports, particularly in the light of the recent disasters in the neighbourhood of Newark. However, attention has been drawn very properly to the features of the bill which pertain to compensation for those whose use of their property is going to be detrimentally affected by the regulations which will be made in pursuance of the powers conferred by this legislation.
In my submission the language of the bill with reference to the basis of compensation is unduly narrow. Account should be taken of the fact that power is given by the bill to limit or restrict not simply the height and location of buildings but their use. If the use of buildings is interfered with it may give rise to a form of damage which cannot be measured in terms of the reduction in the value of the land. It must be measured

Aeronautics Act
also in many cases in terms of loss of business profit or the prospect of business profit. I am sure the minister is well acquainted with the problem that arises in compensation cases where in one class of case the [DOT]claimant is limited to the reduction in the value of his land and in other cases is permitted to make a claim as well for loss of business profit.
It seems to me this is a situation where the widest basis of claim should be permitted, and where anyone who happens to suffer a business loss, quite apart from reduction in the value of his land, in consequence of zoning carried on in pursuance of the powers conferred by the bill, should be entitled to compensation for that type of loss as well as for the reduction in the value of his property.
My second observation relates to the period of limitation of claims. There are not a few statutes, both federal and provincial, where a similar period of limitation is imposed upon claims. In this case it is one year. I think if you will examine most of these other cases you will find that the date from which the period of limitation runs is a date clearly defined and by its nature bound to be known at once to the person who is about to make the claim. That is not the type of situation we have under the bill. The year begins to run not from the date of some physical injury sustained by the claimant, some incident that impresses upon his mind at once that he may have a claim, but, if you please, the period of limitation runs from the date of deposit of the regulation. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra points out that it is not even from the date of the advertisement.
The deposit of the regulation is something that may not come to the attention of a person who has property in the vicinity of the airport for months and months afterwards. It is not something that impresses itself upon his mind. It is not something that comes directly to his notice. Therefore the circumstances contemplated here are not at all to be compared with the circumstances upon which periods of limitation fixed by certain provincial and dominion statutes are based. Accordingly I would urge that these provisions, both in defining the scope of compensation, which is unduly narrow, and the period of limitation, which is unduly short, should be reviewed and revised when the bill goes to the committee. Otherwise I predict now that hardship is going to be suffered by many people. It may be that the government is animated in this situation by the best of intent, but what would happen is what has happened in other situations where cases of hardships arise

and are put before the department. The minister will feel he is bound to take this stand: "This is what the legislation says, and I cannot make exceptions. It is true that hardship results, but I am powerless to deal with it unless I am going to open the door to a great many claims for compassionate consideration."
A period of one year, Mr. Speaker, is very short. It is altogether too short in normal cases unless the nature of the claim is such that it impresses itself forcibly upon the mind of the person in whose favour the claim arises. That is not the situation here. Therefore I would urge not only that some better definition be written into the act of the time from which the period of limitation is to run but also that the period of limitation be extended. I am sure I am not alone in this house in having had professional experience of the way in which these altogether too short periods of limitation in our statutes very often work to the detriment of people who have otherwise legitimate claims. It cannot be said that these unduly short periods of limitation are necessary to protect the public interest. Very often it is simply a case of cutting off claims on an arbitrary basis so that government departments will not have to be bothered by the possibility of claims hanging over the department for a period of time beyond a year or so.
It seems to me that what we should have uppermost in our minds is the desire to do justice to people who are sustaining damage as a result of steps taken in pursuance of statutory authority by the government in the general public interest. It seems to me that the language in which the bill is drawn in that respect at the present time is bound to create hardship in many cases. I offer these suggestions in the hope that the minister will give them serious consideration, and that when the bill goes to the committee it may be revised accordingly.

In doing so I shall try to keep in mind the ruling of His Honour the Speaker.
This is a simple bill. While the zoning regulations may be somewhat complicated I am afraid there is some misapprehension about the application of the restrictions. I should like to deal with that because it is dependent upon the matter of compensation which follows. There seems to be an idea in the minds of hon. members that this legislation is going to affect far more people than in fact it will. It is intended by this bill to create three zoning areas or restrictive areas surrounding airports. The first is that within a radius of 13,000 feet from the centre of an airport no building shall rise to a height of more than 150 feet. My information is that at airports such as Malton and Dorval no building exists that would be in contravention of that zoning regulation.
The second zoning restriction is that in the approaches at the end of the runways having a width of 1,200 feet at the runway end, by a depth of 10,000 feet, and a width of 4,000 feet at the outer end, no building shall rise more than one foot for every 50 feet out. In the third area on the lateral slopes of the flightways no building shall rise more than one foot for every 7 feet out.
I am not able to say how these restrictions will affect different airports such as Vancouver, Malton, Dorval and the like, but it is my understanding that the results of this
Aeronautics Act
legislation will not be nearly as serious as seems to be the thought of some hon. members.

Subsection 5 does two things. Some years ago a system of progressive increases in rates of pay was established. A new punishment known as "forfeiture of service toward progressive increase in pay" was provided for in the National Defence Act. Regulations governing the administration of this punishment proved to be impracticable and consequently, when the Queen's regulations under the National Defence Act were promulgated, it was decided that the
