I would like an answer from the parliamentary assistant. If he cannot give it now perhaps he will let me know in a couple of days how far the commanding officer can go down the line before he reaches the point where he cannot delegate the authority to a junior officer. I would not want to think that this house was going to pass an amendment under which a second lieutenant, or a lieutenant in a junior command, could give a man fourteen days. I would like to have that information.
Canadian Forces Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is my understanding that the commanding officer, subject to approval, can give punishments up to 90 days detention, but under this subsection as it is now proposed he cannot delegate the giving of punishment by a junior officer beyond 14 days detention, and the lesser punishments to which I have already referred.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Does the accused still have the right to ask for a court martial in this case? If there is a summary trial before the commanding officer or a junior officer where he is going to be sentenced to detention, has he the right to ask for a court martial?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: As I understand it under the new code of service discipline, a private has no right under the circumstances mentioned by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano to ask for a court martial, but a non-commissioned officer would, as detention automatically involves reduction in rank.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My recollection of the last war is that in a case where the commanding officer was going to pass punishment which affected the man's pocketbook, as a detention does, he asked the man this question: Are you going to accept my punishment? The hon. member for Nanaimo will confirm me in that, I am sure. Then, with respect to the point raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond and myself, in the case of a man being sentenced to 14 days, has he not the right to ask for a full court martial as he had before? Then there is the other point raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, to how junior an officer can these powers be delegated to put a man away for 14 days?

Before this subsection passes I should like an undertaking that we will get some information on it. I am surprised that the hon. member for Nanaimo has not raised some question on this because no one in the house has more experience in these matters than he has. I have taken men up in front of junior officers for punishment, and I would not want to see this power delegated to those ranks by any amendment. Before this amendment goes through I should like to have a full understanding from the department that this authority is not to be delegated to junior officers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The regulations provide that the authority may not be delegated to officers below the rank of captain in the army and an equivalent rank in the other services.
I would take it that this amendment has to do with captains handling these matters, and that is quite satisfactory.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Would that delegation of power apply in the case of a detachment commander of lower rank than a captain?
2416

Canadian Forces Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am informed that under the Queen's regulations the detachment commander has the same power as the C.O., subject to the C.O. in his case having approved of his having that power.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: So that in such a case the detachment commander can be and very often is an officer junior in the army to a captain or a similar rank?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It could be in that case, yes.

On subsection 17.

We would like to get an
explanation, because this is the most important subsection of these whole amendments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In August of 1949 the
Geneva conventions were entered into. I think they were instituted under the leadership of the Red Cross and resulted from a conference held under the aegis of the Swiss government. They provided for, I think it may be said, the creation or the definition of a series of new crimes called grave breaches, such as torture, biological experiment, and generally a type of crime that I suppose arose in the second world war from the activities of the nazis and from the same type of crime perpetrated by the communists, and which have come to be quite widespread. These conventions provide that countries which subscribe to the conventions agree to enact legislation to enable them to bring persons guilty of such crimes before their courts. In other words the people who have charge of such persons are to be charged with the responsibility of bringing them to trial. Canada has not yet subscribed to the Geneva conventions; but in the event that such action is taken it will be necessary to have certain provisions in the National Defence Act to establish the authority of Canadian tribunals to try alleged offenders. In the opinion of the authorities in the departments of justice, of external affairs and of national defence, such trials, if held in Canada, should take place in the civil courts. The two subsections I had stand over, and this subsection 17, seek to provide the legislation which would make the sanctions of the Geneva conventions operative, if subscribed to by Canada.
Is it not rather unusual to put on the statute books legislation in connection with an international treaty which, I understood the parliamentary assistant to say, had not been ratified by Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The last section of the bill provides that those sections dealing with grave breaches under the Geneva conventions of 1949 will not be effective so far as Canada is concerned unless and until brought into effect by the governor in council. That, of course, would only be in the event that the Geneva conventions are ratified by Canada.

Would these regulations apply to a person who was not a citizen of Canada, but was residing here? I am referring to a foreigner who is not one of our nationals, but who committed a crime in Canada? Would it also apply to a Canadian national, if the crime were committed outside Canada? In that event, would that Canadian national be tried by a Canadian court martial, or would he be tried by the court of the country in which the crime was committed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If the foreigner were in Canada he would be tried here in Canada by the civil courts. But if a Canadian citizen were abroad, then under the terms of the Geneva convention he could be tried by the country by which he is held in custody if it, too, were a subscriber to the conventions. Or he could be handed back to Canada, or tried in any way the country in whose custody he was-that country being a signatory to this convention-should see fit.

Well, may I have a clearer interpretation? Let us say there is a Canadian soldier in Korea or China at the present time who is accused of committing one of these crimes. I think the parliamentary assistant suggested something in connection with germ warfare, when he explained the nature of the crimes. Then do I understand we are agreeing that the Canadian soldier could be tried by a Chinese court, and punished while he is in China? Surely that is taking a very different attitude from that which is being taken now when the United States, or perhaps I should say the United Nations, object to the returning of prisoners of war who do not wish to be returned. This, it seems to me, is going in the very opposite direction. We are saying here that a Canadian who is charged with such a crime as this may be tried by an enemy court, or a court of a country which may at least be only a neutral.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My understanding is that if a citizen of one country that is a party to these conventions, whether he be a soldier or a civilian, were in another country which is also a party to the convention, he could be dealt with by the country in which he is located in regard to these grave breaches of the article of the treaty to which I have referred.
That is, if China were a party to the convention-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; both countries have to be parties to the convention, of course.
Can the parliamentary assistant tell us which countries are signatories to the convention?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: So far the following states have ratified: Chile, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, France, the Holy See, India, Italy, Yugoslavia, Lebanon, Monaco, Norway, Pakistan, Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Jordania.
I notice that neither the United States, the United Kingdom, France nor Canada have signed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Canada has not ratified.

Then I suggest that we are moving too quickly in this matter. A great deal more consideration should be given to it. I asked some questions at the resolution stage, as to whom this applied, and I think we should have some further detailed explanation before we agree to allowing our nationals to be tried in foreign courts for these grave breaches of the Geneva convention. Apparently none of the major nations of the world have agreed to a similar condition.
